Second review: Primes refute the final version; the only prior refutation addresses an earlier, different definition. Short argument.

mo-426204.note: Proves that for every n the corner value making det H_n vanish is unique, and that it tends to 1, answering the question affirmatively against T. Amdeberhan's comment that the limit does not seem to exist. The method is a Gram-matrix argument for binom(i+j,j)^2 on the 2-torus with polynomial approximation of resolvents. My exact computation gives 1/4, 0.349, ..., 0.664 at n=40, a slow (log-like) increase consistent with limit 1. I found no prior solution. Second review: Positive answer via an L2 approximation argument on the torus (Gram matrix of ((1+z)(1+w))^k); numerics consistent. No earlier answer found.

mo-427161.note: Disproof: with jumps X = 2 almost surely, the compound Poisson law gives mass 0 to k=1, while any mixed Poisson law with a density on [0,inf) gives positive mass to 1. Carlo Beenakker's answer also says 'no', but via a variance argument that, as the asker points out, fails for nonnegative integer jumps; the parity example is new on the page and elementary. The counterexample works for any mixing distribution other than the point mass at 0. Second review: Elementary parity counterexample; genuinely unanswered on MO/MSE despite a bounty on MSE.

mo-427595.note: Disproof of the (PB) form of the conjecture with r=2 and f=1/2. At odd dyadic stages W lowers only the middle coefficient by about D/sqrt(n). That keeps |f - B_n(W_n f)| within D M/n (the middle Bernstein basis has height about 1/sqrt n), but breaks (PB) by order 1/sqrt n, more than C M/n for any fixed C. The formal inequality direction and the quantifier order (C depends on W and r, not on f or n) match the source. Second review: Valid counterexample to Peter O.'s consistency conjecture with a slowly converging operator sequence; no earlier answer.

mo-447544.note: Proves that 1+z^p+z^q+z^r-z^n has only simple roots for all 0<p<q<r<n (stronger than the source's 1<p). The method shows a repeated factor is reciprocal, bounds its degree by 6, then uses Landau/Mahler bounds and finite enumeration. No prior proof found: Brunault's comment only reports a search up to n=50, and the Ljunggren argument for the trinomial/quadrinomial sister question does not apply here. I confirmed squarefreeness with sympy for all exponents with n<22. Second review: Positive resolution (all roots simple) by a substantial argument (reciprocal-factor reduction, degree bound 6, finite enumeration). No earlier proof found.

mo-468166.note: Statement 2*sum x_i^{2n} - (sum x_i^n)^2 equals sum x^{2n} - 2*sum_{i<j} x_i^n x_j^n, matching the question's unordered-pair convention, both global signs, all |A|>=4 and n>=1, over C. The question has no answers; Dave Benson's comments only report Magma irreducibility for |A|=4, n<=500 and a belief, not a proof. Short argument; no prior proof found. Second review: Negative answer for every n and every set of at least 4 variables; previously only computational evidence in comments.

mo-476014.note: Counterexample f=1+x+sqrt(x), g=1+x, s=1/2, a=1, b=2: f is 1/2-convex in the second sense, g<=f<=2g, f not convex. Statement matches the question (s in (0,1], positive functions on R_+). No answers or comments on the question; easy counterexample, no prior settlement found. Second review: Trivial explicit counterexample to an unanswered question.

mo-492060.note: Disproof for n=4, k=3: the Fano plane minus one line is intersecting, covers all points, and meets every 5-set (each pair meets only 5 of 7 lines, so 2 lines avoid it), but the pair {0,1} lies in no block, so it is not S(2,3,7). The definitions match the question's three conditions and k<=n-1. The question has no answers and the MSE cross-post was deleted; no prior counterexample found. Second review: Smallest-case counterexample (Fano minus a line) to the asker's conjecture; the asker's own partial proof assumed every pair is covered.

mo-503314.note: Proves emiliocba's conjecture for every odd d (Ikeda had settled only odd prime d) through a Franz-type analysis via Dirichlet characters and a CRT/fibre induction that handles the case where +-r^u-1 is not coprime to m. The statement matches the question's hypotheses (gcd(m,d)=1, order d, gcd(r_i-1,m)=1, identity for all k). The question has no answers, and a comment rejects an AI-generated attempt. No prior resolution found in searches. Second review: Proof of the odd-d conjecture via nonvanishing of character sums of log|1-e(w)| (an L(1,psi) argument); consistent with exhaustive search.

opg-a-funcoid-related-to-directed-topolo.note: Disproof of Porton's conjecture that R meet^FCD (>=) is complete on the extended real line. X = odd positive integers and Y = union of intervals (2n,2n+1) are related by the meet, through the funcoid 'frequently point_n in U and in cl V', which lies below both R and >=. But no single point 2n+1 has its right neighbourhood meeting Y, so completeness fails. Encoding checked: funcoids as binary-additive relations, meet = union of lower bounds, complete = union-preserving. No resolution found on OPG or in Porton's 2023 book. Second review: Valid disproof of Porton's conjecture by an accumulation-at-infinity witness. Short argument once the funcoid encoding is accepted.

opg-atomicity-of-the-poset-of-multifunco.note: Disproves atomisticity for multifuncoids (staroids) on (P Bool)^N. For any atom a, intersecting a with the shift-invariant tail condition 'false occurs at arbitrarily large coordinates' gives a nonzero sub-multifuncoid containing the top tuple, so every atom satisfies it. Hence the nonempty-tuples multifuncoid is not the join of its atoms (the tuple of all {true} escapes). Definitions match the OPG page. Porton's Nov 2023 book still lists atomicity/atomisticity of staroids on powersets as open (Conjectures 2065-2066, 2040-2043). Second review: Atomisticity fails for infinite arity; disproof correct. Finite-arity case is untouched, but the conjecture as posed quantifies over all sets n.

oeis-a001518.note: Proves Peter Bala's Dec 2025 conjecture that (e.g.f. of y_n(3)) / (1 + integral of it) = e.g.f. of A011781. Fidelity checked: recurrence, initial values and the n+1 shift. It is immediate from Salvy's e.g.f. exp(1/3 - sqrt(1-6x)/3)/sqrt(1-6x) in the same entry: the integral is exp(1/3 - sqrt(1-6x)/3) - 1, so the ratio is (1-6x)^(-1/2). Routine; no recorded proof found (not in Blanco Gomez's collection). Second review: Faithful and true. Two-line consequence of the classical Bessel-polynomial e.g.f. listed in the entry, so routine; no explicit earlier proof found.

mo-198816.note: Disproof. Faithful encoding (P*1 = row sums; diagonal dominance read row-wise, but the 13x13 witness is strictly positive, column stochastic and strictly diagonally dominant by rows and by columns, so either reading is covered). Numerically rho(P - P1w^T) = 1.00028 > 1, matching the exact complex eigenpair in the proof. The question has no answers or comments; no prior counterexample found. Second review: Valid 13x13 counterexample (lazy chain with sink) to the asker's numerically supported belief.

mo-201121.note: Disproof of the asker's conjecture that no such f exists for 2 <= n < N-2: an explicit table for N = 8, n = 5, checked by decide and re-checked independently in Python (f(A) in A, and f(A) != f(B) whenever |A cap B| = 4). Consistent with Petrov's answer (N < n + p, p = 5). Statement faithful (n = 1 excluded correctly as trivial). No prior counterexample in the thread; a small finite search witness. Second review: Explicit counterexample at (N,n)=(8,5), consistent with Petrov's partial bound; finite check.

mo-201359.note: Proves the existence of a universal alpha > 0 (about 1/102400) with Area(C1 cap B) >= alpha Area(C cap B) for every compact convex C with nonempty interior, a shortest area-bisecting chord (minimal over all bisecting lines), and every disk centered in C1. Encoding faithful (closed sides share a null line); the conjectured 1/4 is explicitly left out, matching the source's main ask. No answers on MO; the linked question 201181 concerns angles only. Second review: Positive answer (existence of a universal alpha; the asker's 1/4 refinement not claimed). Numerics agree; no earlier answer.

mo-215301.note: Faithful statement (distinct positive denominators, total n, no proper subset with positive integer sum, sums in Q). The proof gives a genuine construction for every n (odd primes up to a bound, one connecting denominator, Stewart's binary remainder method keeping the p-adic markers), and the header credits the precursors honestly. Unanswered on MO; Przezdziecki's answer to MO 209958 only handles repetitions; no distinct-set result found in Erdos-problem literature or Palomar. Second review: Positive answer for distinct reciprocals via primes plus a Stewart-type remainder; previously only the repeated-denominator version and n=2 ad hoc were known.

mo-227558.note: The eight equations say only that the six unit vectors have centroid 0 and second-moment matrix 2I. A triangular prism (z = +-1/sqrt3, theta = 0, +-2pi/3 on both levels) satisfies them but is not an octahedron, since the antipode of the first vertex is missing. That refutes the asked 'only if' direction. John Jiang's comment only suspected a missing equation from a dimension count; the explicit counterexample is new but elementary. Second review: The 'only if' direction is false: a prism satisfies all eight moment equations. Finite verification.

mo-232032.note: Read as 'a strict decrease of JSD between two pairs forces a strict decrease of KL(P||Q)', refuted with Bernoulli coins: (0.9, 0.7) -> (0.9, 0.99) lowers JSD while KL rises from 0.116 to 0.145. The question is loose, but this is the natural formal reading. The failure is folklore-level, and unanswered on MO. Second review: A correct and elementary disproof of a vague MO question. With KL in the order P relative to Q, as the question writes it, the example works. In the reverse order the same example would not work, but the question fixes the order.

mo-286619.note: The sharp constant alpha = 2(n/(n+1))^n/(n+1) |P| (IsLeast of int|f| over convex mean-zero f with inf -1) is correct: a translated Minkowski-gauge cone attains it, and homothetic sublevel sets give the lower bound. It matches |P|/2 at n = 1, the asker's examples (8/27 < 0.395 for the triangle), and my hand computation. fedja (answer 280462 to the linked question) said the sharp constant follows by a similar short argument but never wrote it, so the explicit value is new on MO, though routine. Second review: The formula agrees exactly with the MO examples and with the fact that the extremal is a cone. No prior closed form was found, and the Lean proof covers both bound and attainment.

Erdos889.erdos_889.variants.v1_eq_1_fini.note: The formal statement ({n | sup_{k>=1} v(n,k) = 1} is finite) faithfully encodes the lowercase-v_1 question of Erdős-Selfridge. It is solved via reduction R1 with H1 (finite window, @ivillar), H2 (odd case, @dk8827) and H3 (even case by a polynomial/weighted-power argument, @MrSeizy), all on main. Kitamura's FC PR 6453 only did capital V_1, which does not imply this since v <= V, and the forum says explicitly that lowercase v_1 stays open. I found nothing on conjectures.io, in Palomar or in FC PRs. Second review: A real research result: the open 1967 question of Erdos and Selfridge on lowercase v_1, with an effective bound. The pieces are credited to site contributors (@MrSeizy, @rorcores, @ivillar). The statement is the faithful FC one, and no earlier solution exists according to erdosproblems.com and its forum.

arxiv-1803.00823.note: I checked the formal definitions against Section 2 of the source: M_n with P+P^T=1, symmetry under relabelling, honesty at every reachable match for every P, A_n the closure of achievable vectors with P doubly monotonic, and the G_n Rules 1-3. They are faithful. The disproof is an explicit 4-player, 5-match symmetric and honest tournament whose strongest player wins with probability < 1/4, while every point of A*_4 has first coordinate >= 1/4. The source itself says it is open whether min pi_1 = 1/n for n >= 4. The only earlier hint is the contributor's unproved computation in the site's statement PR 8195; I found no published refutation. Second review: The Lean disproof exhibits a symmetric honest 4-player tournament in which the strongest player wins with probability below 1/n. The paper explicitly leaves this question open (Pi_{1,n}=1/n?). The definitions follow the paper closely.

arxiv-1810.07219.note: The formal A(x) (functions on positions with no fixed letter and the right letter counts) and the hypothesis 'exists m, x_i < x_m' match Bangachev's Conjecture 6.0.1 verbatim; the source only proves it when x_i < max/2. The proof is a genuine coefficient-positivity argument on prod_j (sum_{k≠j} t_k)^{x_j}. I found no prior proof: Gonçalves (arXiv:2609.31979) cites the paper only for the balancing Theorem 4.3. Second review: The conjecture was open in the source, with only a partial result there. The one later paper citing the source proves a different (majorization) statement. The numerical check agrees with the proof.

mo-121243.note: The statement uses the zero-diagonal adjacency matrix of the Fibonacci-sum graph, as clarified in the question edit and comments, with det = 0 for odd n and det ∈ {0,±1} for even n. The odd case already follows from bipartiteness (Arman-Gunderson-Li, arXiv:1710.10303). The even case had only a partial MSE answer (D'Aurizio 2014) and is proved here by a leaf-elimination determinant recurrence. I found no prior full proof. Second review: Open since 2013, with only partial ideas on MSE. The proof cites D'Aurizio's forced-partner observation and gives credit for it.

mo-130917.note: The statement is a faithful transcription of the asked inequality for all p > 1. The MO answers give only a heuristic second-derivative sketch ('the other regions can probably be taken care of similarly') and the even-integer case, so there was no complete proof. The Lean proof is an elementary case analysis (near-diagonal mean-value bound plus large-|x| estimates). Second review: Only heuristics were given before. The Lean proof is a short elementary estimate.

mo-145467.note: The statement is a faithful transcription of Wolfgang's 'prove or disprove' inequality sum (1-a_i)/(1-a_i^{λn}) >= (1-r)/(1-r^λ) with r = prod a_i^c and c = (λ-1/n)/(λ-1), with the continuous value 1/s at t=1. It covers all real λ > 1 and a_i >= 0. Neither the MO question (tagged open-problems) nor the MSE crosspost has an answer, and I found no published proof. The proof is a genuine Jensen-type argument on x/(e^x-1). Second review: This was a 'prove or disprove' with no answers anywhere. It is proved in full generality in Lean, and the high-precision tests are consistent.

mo-194396.note: The statement faithfully encodes the edited question (all α_i, β_i, γ_i nonzero, periodic tridiagonal of size n >= 3, Fin wrap-around placing β_n and γ_n in the corners). The only answer gives an n=2 example with a zero entry, and the nonzero case was left open in the comments. The disproof uses α=(2,2,-1), β=(1,-2,1), γ=(1,1,-2), giving A = I + nilpotent with charpoly (λ-1)^3 (I checked it is not diagonalizable), so no similarity makes it normal. Correct but routine. Second review: Correct and elementary. The obstruction is the same one as in the existing n=2 answer (non-diagonalizability), now with all coefficients nonzero as the edit requires, so it is routine. I did not treat it as a pre-existing answer because the MO answer has zero entries.

oeis-a054118.note: Mathar's recurrence a(n)=(n+1)a(n-1)-n a(n-2) for n>=6 is stated faithfully: the triangle T follows A054115's row-sum rule, a(n)=T(n,n-3) with offset 3 reproduces the data, and I checked the recurrence for n<60. No proof found in the entry, its cross-references, the proof collections or the Lean libraries. Routine manipulation of the row-sum recursion. Second review: A routine recurrence identity (row-sum ratio). It was not proved before for this subdiagonal.

oeis-a054516.note: Mathar's homogeneous recurrence is stated for every n>=5 with the entry's first-order definition a(3)=0, a(n)=-(n-3)a(n-1)+(n-3)(n-2). The definition reproduces the data, and I checked the identity for n<60. Routine elimination from the first-order recurrence. No prior proof found. Second review: Mathar's homogeneous recurrence follows by substitution from the defining recurrence. Routine.

oeis-a057081.note: Bala's general conjecture (for k>=1, Sum_{n>=1} (-1)^(n+1)/(a(kn)-s(k)/a(kn)) = 1/(1+a(k)), where s(k)=a(0)+...+a(k-1)) is stated faithfully, with a(n)=U_{2n}(sqrt(11)/2) and the source index n=j+1. I checked the partial sums numerically for k=1..4. The entry proves only the k=1 case (1/11). No prior proof of the general case found. The proof uses Binet forms and telescoping. Second review: A telescoping identity for a C-finite sequence. Routine and not previously proved for m=11.

oeis-a058347.note: The symmetry conjecture T(n,k)=T(k,n) is stated for the entry's explicit recurrence (Formula section). The Lean cases n=1 and k=1 are correct specializations of it, it reproduces all 52 data terms (read by antidiagonals), and I checked symmetry for n,k<15. No prior proof found. The proof normalizes by 2^(nk) and shows the transposed recurrence holds. Routine. Second review: A recurrence identity, so routine. Small residual doubt: van Dongen's later thesis might contain the symmetry; I found no evidence of that.

oeis-a059135.note: Barker's closed form -53+2^(6+n)-21n, recurrence and g.f. are stated faithfully, with W2{3} phrases following Wallgren's note. The definition reproduces the data, and I checked the closed form for n<15. The entry has no proof. It is the same easy self-similarity argument that Neder recorded for the sister entry A059133. Routine. Second review: A closed form via the 2-adic valuation and Legendre's formula. Routine.

oeis-a059442.note: A disproof of Luo's fence conjecture at m=n=65536. Erdos's probabilistic bound gives R(m,m) > 2^(m/2), while T(3m-6,m) <= p(196602) <= 2^18432, so (2m-1)T+m+1 < R. The encoding (least N forcing an m-clique or an independent n-set, and partitions into exactly m parts as in A008284) is faithful. The proof adapts only a lemma (the probabilistic lower bound) from an earlier on-site Erdos #78 proof, not an earlier refutation. I found no prior refutation. The counterexample is conceptually easy: exponential versus subexponential growth. Second review: The disproof is a short argument from Erdos's classical lower bound against the subexponential growth of the partition numbers. It is correct but not deep. Nobody had recorded it in the entry.

oeis-a059804.note: For n>=19, d*(v.v) = A024450(n-1), where d is the least squared distance from a lattice point other than 0 and v to the segment [0,v]. The segment reading is forced by 'excluding the endpoints'. Points that project outside the segment are farther away than e_n, so the line and segment readings agree. The data a(19..38) equal the stated sums. The entry says 'Officially these are just conjectures', and the Fat Struts papers do not treat the prime vector. The proof is substantive: geometry plus explicit prime-counting estimates. Second review: The entry itself says 'officially these are just conjectures'. The Lean proof uses prime-counting estimates and finite windows. I found no prior proof.

oeis-a060903.note: Wilson's conjecture, sigma(n) < floor(6 n sqrt(n)/pi^2) for n>12, is stated faithfully. I checked it numerically for 13 <= n < 10^5. The proof uses sigma(n) <= n(1+log n) for n>=100 and decide below. No prior proof found. Routine. Second review: A short bound sigma(n) <= n(1+log n) plus a finite check. Routine.

oeis-a061002.note: Detlefs's identity den(H(p)/H(p-1)) = p^3 * num(H(p-1)/p^2) for primes p>3 is stated faithfully. I checked it for p<200. It is a short consequence of Wolstenholme's theorem (cited in the entry): with H(p-1)=A/B, p^2|A and p not dividing B, one gets H(p)/H(p-1) = (pA+B)/(pA) in lowest terms. The proof formalizes Wolstenholme and this step. Routine, not definitional. Second review: A three-line consequence of Wolstenholme's theorem, which the entry cites. Routine.

oeis-a061262.note: The statement is the conjunction of Cloitre's growth conjecture and Sun's mod-5 conjecture. 'ways' (unordered i<=j<=k, 0 triangular) reproduces ways(57)=6 and the first 12 data terms. The disproof is genuine: it does not use the sInf-of-empty value. It shows that ways(m) > 48 sqrt(m) for arbitrarily large counts, so a(n) <= m < n^2 infinitely often, refuting Cloitre's lower bound (the conjunction then fails). No prior refutation found. The construction (odd-square reflections mod 3) is nontrivial. Second review: A valid disproof of Cloitre's part; Sun's part plays no role. The computation already shows ratios below 1 at n near 1900. No prior refutation found.

oeis-a064377.note: Completeness of the 111 listed solutions of sigma_4(n) > phi(n)^5 is stated faithfully: the Finset equals the OEIS data, and my own search to 2*10^5 finds exactly those 111. Greathouse's comment proves only finiteness. The proof gives explicit prime-power bounds and a finite check. Routine. Second review: An effective bound plus a finite check. Routine, but completeness had not been proved before.

oeis-a071055.note: Stephan's b(n+1) recurrence and Hüffner's pext(n,n+1) formula are stated faithfully for the Rule 182 triangle (182's bit table, single ON cell, row positions -n..n, unbounded pext). My Rule 182 simulation reproduces the data, and both formulas hold for n<300. No prior proof found. Routine: the structure is self-similar, Sierpinski-like. Second review: Both conjectured formulas hold. The pattern is the known Sierpinski-type triangle, so this is routine. No rule-182 theorem exists in the Lean CA libraries.

oeis-a072523.note: McGarvey's two limits (F(n)/a(n) -> sqrt5/2 and a(n)/a(n-1) -> phi) are stated faithfully: the divisors are F(m) for 3 <= m < n, i.e. Fibonacci numbers greater than 1 and smaller than F(n). The definition reproduces the data, and the ratios match the limits numerically up to n=200. No prior proof found. Routine Binet and remainder analysis. Second review: Asymptotics of F(n) mod F(n-j) via the Fibonacci addition formula. Correct, and no prior proof was found.

oeis-a074354.note: Barker's g.f. and order-8 recurrence (n>10) for the q^3 coefficient of nu(n) with (b,lambda)=(1,2) are stated faithfully, and the nu recursion matches the name. I checked the data, the g.f. to x^30 and the recurrence. Routine coefficient-extraction g.f. argument, consistent with the earlier confirmations of A074358/A074359. Second review: A g.f. identity for a rational g.f. Routine.

oeis-a075125.note: Mathar's P-recurrence is stated for n>=5 with a(n) defined as the coefficients of the entry's algebraic g.f. (S = binomial-series sqrt of the radicand). The g.f. reproduces all 35 data terms. Each of the five expanded Lean polynomial coefficients equals Mathar's factored ones, and the recurrence holds to n=40. Routine: a holonomic certificate derived from S^2 = R. Second review: A routine holonomic recurrence for an algebraic g.f. (the EYZ method covers it), but not previously proved for this entry.

oeis-a079269.note: Quet's numerator recurrence a(m+1) = a(m)^2 + a(m)^3/(2a(m-1)^2) - a(m)a(m-1)^2/2 (m>=2, rational divisions) is stated with a(n) = num(b(n)) and the source offset. I checked the data and the identity for m<12 with exact rationals. trureturing proves only the companion denominator recurrence (A079278) and explicitly says it does not claim the A079269 numerator one. No other prior proof found. Routine algebra from b -> b(b+2)/(b+1). Second review: A numerator recurrence from b' = b(2b+1)/(b+1) and coprimality. Routine.

oeis-a004257.note: Kurkov's identity round(log_2 n) = A000523(n^2) - A000523(n) is stated faithfully (Real.logb, Mathlib round = floor(x+1/2), Nat.log 2). It is Hermite's identity floor(2x) - floor(x) = floor(x + 1/2) at x = log_2 n, so it is routine. I checked it exactly for n < 200000. No prior written proof found in the entry, the libraries, the proof collections or Palomar. Second review: Faithful. Kurkov's conjecture is an immediate instance of Hermite's identity, so it is trivially true but not vacuous. No prior written proof located.

oeis-a006134.note: Wiseman's two marked identities a(n) = A013580(2n+1,n+1) and a(n) = A231147(2n+1,n+1) are encoded with the right coordinate shifts: one-based rows/medians and integer-median columns at even positions. Checked against the printed triangles. Both are one-line coefficient extractions: from Jovovic's g.f. 1/((1-(1+y)x)(1-yx^2)) for A013580, and from [x^j](1+x^2)^j for the numerator of p(N,x+1/x). So the 77-line proof is routine. No prior written proof found. Second review: Faithful; both identities are short g.f. consequences of formulas already in the entries. No prior proof located.

oeis-a008366.note: Detlefs' characterization (n > 1 divides both Sum k^10 and Sum k^12 iff minFac(n) >= 17) is stated faithfully, and it holds for n < 5000. The proof clears Faulhaber's formula (denominators 66 and 2730, with constant terms 5 and -691 coprime to them). That is the standard von Staudt-Clausen-type argument, so it is routine. No proof found in the entry, its sister rough-number entries (the analogous A008364 power-sum conjecture is still open there), the libraries or the proof collections. Second review: Faithful and true; short number-theoretic argument (p-1 | 10 or 12 for p<=13, plus prime-power lifting). No prior proof found.

oeis-a023861.note: Voznyy's 2009 rational g.f. for the weighted Lucas sums a(n) = Sum_{k<floor((n+1)/2)} (k+1) L(n-k) is encoded faithfully, with the sign normalized and the denominator cleared. I checked the definition against the data and the identity to 60 terms. The proof handles the even and odd cases of the cutoff with recurrences, so it is routine. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful rational g.f. identity, routine. No prior proof found.

oeis-a023871.note: Bala's supercongruence u(np^r) = u(np^{r-1}) mod p^{3r} for p >= 7 (u(n) = [x^n] A(x)^n, A truncated at k <= n, which is harmless) is stated faithfully. I checked p = 7, 11, 13 with r = 1 and p = 7 with r = 2; it fails at p = 5 as expected. The prescreen hit is rbajaj5/a183068-supercongruence. Its campaign table (current main) lists A023871 only as 'partial': the p^{2r} baseline is proved, but the Cartier-square bound needed for p^{3r} remains open there. The 1993-line site proof establishes the full p^{3r} tower via the Cartier-square estimate, so it goes beyond the public partial result. Second review: Faithful statement of Bala's p>=7 cubic supercongruence; the strongest public prior work (rbajaj5) explicitly leaves it open. Deep result, not routine.

oeis-a024385.note: Mathar's recurrence (n >= 9, offset 1) and g.f. for floor(e2/e1) of the first n+1 numbers = 1 mod 4 are stated faithfully: a(0) = 0 is padding, and the sign of the g.f. is normalized. Both hold to n = 300, and the recurrence fails at n = 8 only through the padding, so the range is right. The proof writes e1 and e2 as polynomials and then evaluates the floor of their ratio, which is routine. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful, routine quasi-polynomial/g.f. identity. No prior proof found.

oeis-a024459.note: Mathar's 2020 g.f. for Sum_{k<floor((n+1)/2)} F(k+1) L(n-k) is stated faithfully, with the sign normalized and the denominator cleared; it agrees with the data and holds to 80 terms. The proof is the same parity-split recurrence argument as A023861, so it is routine. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful rational g.f., routine. No prior proof found.

oeis-a025093.note: Barker's 2019 g.f. and order-10 recurrence are stated for the data-consistent reading of the name: a(n) = Sum_{i<=floor((n+1)/2)} L(i)(2(n-i)+3), offset 1, a(0) = 0. The statement documents this reading, and it matches all listed terms; the literal name does not. The identity is a routine parity-split Lucas computation (168 lines). No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful to Barker's conjecture about the listed terms; the name/data offset discrepancy in OEIS is handled openly. Routine.

oeis-a026021.note: Mathar's recurrence is printed with a missing operator ('... a(n-3) 44*(n-3)*(7n-27)*a(n-4)'). I checked that +44, -44 and +4 all fail from n = 4, while -4 makes it hold for every n in 4..79, so the statement's reading is forced. Marinov's T(n,k) = C(n,k) - C(n,k-3) matches the recursive A026009 array. The proof reduces both parities to central binomials (the same method as the site's A026008 proof), which is routine. Second review: Faithful up to an unavoidable, disclosed repair of a garbled coefficient (-4 is the only value that makes the identity true). Routine P-recursive identity.

oeis-a028355.note: Chai Wah Wu's 2024 recurrence a(n) = 1000001 a(n-15) - 1000000 a(n-30) and g.f. for the Orloj sequence are stated faithfully (digit stream 1,2,3,4,3,2 cut into groups of sum n). I checked them to n = 120. The proof uses the period-6 / 15-group structure of the stream, so it is routine. The site also solved the sister conjectures A028359 and A068962; no external prior proof found. Second review: Faithful and routine once the period-15/6-digit structure is shown. No prior proof found.

oeis-a028884.note: Purath's a(n) = A079896(A265284(n-1)) is stated with A079896 at offset 0, the offset in force when the conjecture was made (Jan 2023; Sloane changed it to 1 in Mar 2023). I checked it for n < 300. thatnealpatel/proofs only refutes the current-offset reading and checks the shifted identity for n <= 8 'not proved for all indices', so the site proof is the first full proof. It is a routine Rule 94 pattern plus discriminant counting. Second review: Faithful under the historically correct offset; the only public prior work refutes the anachronistic offset-1 reading. Elementary (CA shape plus discriminant counting) but not a pure finite check.

oeis-a033627.note: Ya-Ping Lu's conjecture is stated faithfully: for every n >= 1, the number of distinct tail-plus-cycle lengths of m -> m^2+1 on Z/10^n equals a(n+1) of the greedy 0-additive sequence, with distinct pairs as the data requires. I checked n <= 6 by brute force (2, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16). The proof shows f^[3n+3] = f^[3n-3] on Z/10^n using 2-adic contraction and a 5-adic valuation gain every three steps, and exhibits a point with maximal tail. That is a genuine argument. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful and nontrivial; no prior proof found.

oeis-a047968.note: Adams-Watters' 2014 conjecture that Sum_{d|n} p(d) is strictly increasing for n > 6 is stated faithfully: a(m) < a(n) for 7 <= m < n, and a(6) = 17 > a(7) = 16 shows the threshold. I checked it to n = 3000. The proof builds an explicit injection, valid for n >= 7, from the partitions of divisors of n into those of divisors of n+1 (lift the parts, insert a marker) that misses at least one element. It is elementary but a real construction. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful; requires a uniform bound on p(n+1)-p(n) versus sum of p(d), d<=n/2. No prior proof found.

oeis-a052952.note: Lang's 2012 conjecture floor|F((1+i)(n+2))| = F(n+2) - (n mod 2) for the complex Fibonacci function is stated faithfully (2*phi - 1 = sqrt5 is the denominator). The proof bounds the modulus between (phi^m -+ e^{-pi m} phi^{-m})/sqrt5 and compares with Binet's formula, a short routine argument. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful; a short exponential estimate proves it. Only a trureturing preregistration exists.

oeis-a088039.note: Barker's closed form a(n) = 2^n+1 (n>2), recurrence (n>4) and g.f. 2x-2x^2+x^3-2x^4 over (1-x)(1-2x), with a(0) = 0 and a(n) = least k>1 with b^n | k^3-1 for some b>1. My brute force gives 2,4,9,17,...,16385 for n = 1..14, matching the data. The proof is elementary: cubing is bijective on units mod 2^n, and other prime powers force k > 2^n. Nothing found in the entry, A088038, Palomar, the Lean libraries or the proof collections. Second review: Faithful and routine. No prior proof found.

oeis-a089695.note: Murthy's finiteness conjecture: numbers whose every split into consecutive digit blocks has a prime block-sum. The formalization is faithful (blocks of the ordinary decimal string, one-block split included, leading zeros allowed inside blocks). My brute force up to 10^6 reproduces all 38 data terms. The proof bounds the number of nonzero digits by a mod-11 merging argument, then checks a finite prefix certificate. No prior proof found: the entry only has Wasserman's search to 10^8, and Palomar, the Lean libraries and the proof collections have nothing. Second review: Faithful; the proof bounds digit multiplicities by modular choices and then certifies a finite search. No prior proof found.

oeis-a089696.note: Finiteness of the numbers for which every placement of '*' between digits gives (product of blocks)+1 prime. The formalization is faithful; the offset-0 detail does not matter for finiteness. My brute force up to 10^6 reproduces all 24 data terms (1,...,658). The proof is a full classification: a congruence certificate forces a long word to contain a forbidden configuration, plus a finite search tree. No prior proof found (entry: only Wasserman's search to 10^7; Palomar, the libraries and the collections have nothing). Second review: Faithful finiteness conjecture; no prior proof found.

oeis-a090996.note: Yanev's 2016 formula a(n) = w(n+1)(w(n+1)-w(n)+1) - w(2^(w(n+1)+1)-n-1) for n>0, with w = floor(log2), is stated faithfully (leading ones of the binary expansion; outer arithmetic in Z). I checked it for n < 200000. The proof is an elementary induction on the binary recursion. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful and routine bit identity. No prior proof found.

oeis-a091539.note: Mathar's 2026 recurrence for the explicit triple-factorial closed form in the entry, (prod(3j+2)/10)*(3^n n! - 3 prod(3j+1))/6. The closed form reproduces all 14 data terms and the recurrence holds for 4 <= n < 80 in my check. Both product terms satisfy the recurrence identically, so this is routine. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful and true; a recurrence identity for an explicit closed form (Mathar, Jul 2026). Nothing earlier found.

oeis-a092843.note: Kotesovec's Sum_{k<=n} a(k) ~ n^2/2 for a(n) = Sum_{k|n,k>1} phi(k-1), stated faithfully (IsEquivalent over R). The proof uses the exact identity summatory = n(n+1)/2 - Sum_j phi(floor(n/j)), which I checked for n <= 20000, and bounds the error by n*H_n. Elementary and routine. No prior proof found. Second review: True with a short elementary argument (sum_{d|n} phi(d) = n plus telescoping); marked routine because it is a few-line classical argument, though it uses no fact from the entry itself. No prior proof found.

oeis-a093348.note: Neder's 2019 formula a(n+1) = (n mod 2) + Sum_k 4*5^k*(floor(n/5^(k+1)) mod 2) is stated faithfully, with the castle recursion a(1) = 0, a(n) = w(n) - a(n-w(n)) and the infinite sum truncated correctly. My check reproduces the data and the identity for n < 5000. Routine base-5 digit induction. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful and true; follows by digit induction in base 5 (the entry's formula a(n)=sum (-1)^(i-1)5^v_5(i) makes it a short argument). Nothing earlier found.

oeis-a094187.note: Mathar's 2021 recurrence a(n) = (196n-51)a(n-1) - 2754(n-1)(2n-3)a(n-2). Here a(n) = I(n)*8*9^(2n-1)*(2n-1)!!, with I(n) computed exactly by termwise integration (checked against mpmath quadrature). This reproduces all 13 data terms, so the 'numerator' reading is right, and the recurrence holds for 3 <= n < 40. Routine holonomic identity. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful to the data and program (the name's 'numerator' is loose, but the Lean follows the actual sequence). True, routine.

oeis-a097155.note: The conjecture that 0 and 89 are the only fixed points of f(x) = reverse(x) - maxdigit(x) is formalized faithfully (reversal drops leading zeros, as in the Mathematica program). My search finds only 0 and 89 below 10^6. The proof is elementary: reverse(x) - x is a multiple of 9, so the maximal digit must be 9, and then digit comparisons finish. No prior proof in the sister entries A097153-A097158 or elsewhere. Second review: Faithful and true by a short elementary argument. Nothing earlier found.

oeis-a099237.note: Bala's 2023 congruences a(2^k) = 1 mod 2^k, a(3^k) = 1 mod 3^(k+1) and a(p^k) = 1 mod p^(k+1) (p >= 5), for a(n) = Sum_k C(n(n-k),k), are stated faithfully. I spot-checked small prime powers. The proof is a short Kummer/Pascal argument, C(n(n-k),k) = (-1)^k p^m mod p^(m+1), plus alternating cancellation for odd p. Routine; no prior proof found (entry, A359842, Palomar, libraries, collections). Second review: Faithful and true; a genuine (though one-page, elementary) proof of Bala's congruences, not a finite check, hence routine=false. No prior proof found on the web, GitHub or the proof collections.

oeis-a104041.note: Bala's 2023 closed forms: binomial(n,k-n)(-2)^(2n-k) for even rows and Sum_i S2(n,i) s1(i+2,k+1-n) for odd rows. The statement proves that balaT is unit lower-triangular, has inverse equal to its reversed absolute columns (the entry's defining duality, which matches the A104040 example), and is the unique such triangle under the sign and support conditions. I checked that the g.f. triangle (1-x+xy)/(1+2x^2y-x^2y^2) satisfies those conditions and equals balaT for 24 rows. Indirect but faithful; no prior proof found. Second review: True and faithful; trivially implied by the entry's own g.f., so routine. Minor point for the owner: the uniqueness clause carries an extra sign hypothesis not in the name.

oeis-a104385.note: Stephan's formula a(n) = round((3n^4+6n^3-33n^2-36n+110)/144) for partitions of n(n+1)/2 into 3 distinct positive parts is stated faithfully. My check agrees for n < 120, and the fractional parts are only 1/72, 7/72, 25/72 and 55/72, so the rounding is unambiguous. Quasi-polynomial counting; routine. No prior proof found. Second review: True and faithful; follows from the classical formula for partitions into 3 distinct parts plus a residue check, so routine.

oeis-a104632.note: Mathar's 2017 recurrence for a(n) = [x^(2n+1)](1+x+x^2+x^3+x^4)^n / n (n >= 4) is stated faithfully over Q. My check reproduces the data and the recurrence for 4 <= n < 40. The proof is a routine polynomial/creative-telescoping identity using the reciprocity of the pentanomial. No prior proof found (entry, Banderier et al. 2016 give explicit formulas but not this recurrence; Palomar, libraries, collections). Second review: Faithful, true, routine.

oeis-a105794.note: Schulte's two 2025 conjectures for T = inverse of A105793, with A105793 encoded as the coefficients of (x+1)x(x-1)...(x-n+2). Both are faithful: the inverse reproduces the data, and with B(1) = -1/2, Mathlib's convention and B(n,0), I checked both for n < 16, m < 8. Conjecture 1 is immediate from Bala's comment (x-1)^n = Sum T(n,k) x_(k) evaluated at x = -m-1. Conjecture 2 follows from the Stirling formula for Bernoulli numbers. Routine; no prior proof found. Second review: Faithful and true; both identities are short consequences of the connection-constant description in the entry, so routine.

oeis-a106181.note: Mathar's 2011 recurrence (n+2)a(n) + n a(n-1) + 4(n-1)a(n-2) + 4(n-3)a(n-3) = 0 (n >= 3). The g.f. c(-x^2)(1+2x-sqrt(1+4x^2))/2 is characterized correctly (S^2 = 1+4x^2, S(0) = 1, -2x^2 c = 1-S). It reproduces the data, and the recurrence holds for n < 40. Routine algebraic-g.f. holonomic identity (the terms are signed Catalan numbers). No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful, true, routine.

oeis-a108308.note: Mathar's 2011 order-4 recurrence for the g.f. 1/(1-x^2 c(2x)) is stated faithfully. The g.f. is characterized by S^2 = 1-8x, S(0) = 1, 4x c = 1-S, G(1-x^2 c) = 1, and the coefficient polynomials are expanded correctly. My check reproduces the data and the recurrence for 4 <= n < 45. Routine algebraic-g.f. holonomic identity. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful, true, routine.

oeis-a111097.note: This proves together Alaa's 2026 empirical formula a(n) = n(n+1)/2 - 1 - floor((n-1)/3) (n >= 2), McKone's 2023 second-difference pattern and Spezia's 2026 g.f. The likelihood n*N^(n falling)/N^(n+1) (n distinct draws then a repeat) and the least maximizer are faithful. My exact argmax search reproduces the data and the formula for n < 40. The proof needs careful exact comparisons of neighbouring urn sizes via truncated binomial bounds. No prior proof found (entry, A083704, Palomar, libraries, collections). Second review: Faithful and true for all n; the proof is an elementary but genuine analytic argument, so routine=false. Web search found MLE-of-population-size literature but no exact closed form.

oeis-a112001.note: Mathar's 2017 first-order recurrence for a(n) = A111999(n+4,3)/4. The formal triangle uses A111999's recurrence, and the formalizer rightly reads the formula line's A112492 as a slip for A111999. It reproduces all 16 data terms, and the recurrence holds for 1 <= n < 40. The proof uses closed forms of the first four columns (hypergeometric); routine. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful, true, routine.

oeis-a121696.note: The formal a uses the entry's defining recurrence a(n)=a(n-2)+n(n-2)!floor((n-1)/2), a(1)=0, a(2)=1; the padded a(0) is unused. It reproduces the data. Mathar's a(n)-(n-1)^2a(n-2)-n(n-2)a(n-3)=0 holds for n>=4 (checked to 40). The proof goes via a(m+2)+a(m+1)=(m+1)!floor((m+3)/2). Second review: Faithful; true numerically; routine recurrence manipulation. No prior proof found.

oeis-a121725.note: Mathar's D-finite recurrence for an algebraic g.f.; the rationalized g.f. reproduces the data, and the recurrence (n+1)a(n)=10(n+1)a(n-1)+36(n-2)a(n-2)-360(n-2)a(n-3) checks for n>=3. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful formalization of Mathar's conjectured recurrence for the algebraic g.f.; holds numerically and is a routine holonomic consequence of the g.f. No prior proof found.

oeis-a123516.note: Bala's identity P(n,1/2+x)=p(n,x^2) or x*p(n,x^2), his Conjecture 1 (zeros on Re=1/2, n>=1) and Conjecture 2 (zeros of p(n,u) negative and interlacing, n>=2) are stated faithfully. Root counts are floor(n/2), the ordering is fixed and m>=1. The results reduce to classical Legendre facts: P(n,x) ~ (x^2-x)^(n/2)*P_n((2x-1)/(2sqrt(x^2-x))). I found no published proof (searched OEIS and the web). Second review: Faithful and true; no prior proof found. Caveat for the announcement: both conjectures follow quickly from a classical Legendre-polynomial representation, so this is an easy result rather than a deep one.

oeis-a123722.note: qualifies(m) means #squares mod m = ceil((m+1)/3); 'preceding >= 2' encodes Layman's n>2. My computation reproduces the data, has no composite m/3 among the terms below 3000, and finds 3p qualifying for every odd prime p<900. The proof uses multiplicativity of A000224 and a sharp bound for odd moduli. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful, true, short elementary argument via the known formula for the number of squares mod n. No prior proof found.

oeis-a123723.note: The faithful analogue for ceil((m+1)/4) with n>4 (at least four earlier terms). The data are reproduced, and there are no counterexamples below 3000. The proof (squares mod 4q represented by 0..q, plus a collision u+v vs |u-v| for composite q) is elementary but genuine. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful, true, elementary. No prior proof found.

oeis-a124869.note: a(n) = reduced numerator of Re(((-1-3i)/10)^n) reproduces the data. Both Barker conjectures check to n=80: the g.f. with denominator (1-8x^2+25x^4)(1+8x^2+25x^4), and a(n)=14a(n-4)-625a(n-8) for n>10. The proof controls the 2- and 5-adic cancellation explicitly. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful and true; routine (denominator/valuation analysis of a rational linear recurrence). No prior proof found.

oeis-a126089.note: The e.g.f. (1-2x)sqrt(1-4x) is pinned down by F^2 and constant term 1. Mathar's first-order recurrence (4-n)a(n)+2(2n-5)(n-3)a(n-1)=0 holds for n>=1 and reproduces the data. It is a routine e.g.f. ODE computation, and no prior proof was found. Second review: Faithful formalization of Mathar's conjectured recurrence for the algebraic g.f.; holds numerically and is a routine holonomic consequence of the g.f. No prior proof found.

oeis-a126932.note: Mathar's D-finite recurrence for an algebraic g.f.; Barry's g.f. (sqrt(1-2x-3x^2)+3(1-3x))/(2(2-13x+21x^2)) reproduces the data, and the recurrence matches (n>=3). No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful formalization of Mathar's conjectured recurrence for the algebraic g.f.; holds numerically and is a routine holonomic consequence of the g.f. No prior proof found.

oeis-a128153.note: The model counts translated positive and negative dilates of the pentagon whose 5 side lines come from the two offset progressions in Priluck's second construction (with vertex chords). It is intricate, but my brute force of the model gives 9,20,37,58,85,116,153 for n=1..7, matching the data. Priluck's paper (A128127 PDF) states Z5 = (10p^2+16p+9-(-1)^p)/4 only as a conjecture from experiments. The proof gives the formula, Wu's recurrence and the g.f. Second review: Formula, recurrence and g.f. proved for the modelled count; the model matches all 13 data terms. Residual risk is only model fidelity for larger n, which I could not derive independently in full.

oeis-a128424.note: The formal recurrence is a(n)=floor(sqrt(a(n-1)^2+a(n-2)^2+a(n-1)a(n-2))) with a(1)=1, a(2)=3 (padded a(0)=0). Barker's recurrence (n>7) and g.f. hold: exact computation to n=400, and the data match. The proof shows a(n+4)-1 satisfies b(n+3)=b(n+2)+b(n) with explicit error margins bracketing the square root. No prior proof found. (A020711 agreeing only for n<=41 concerns that Pisot sequence, not this one.) Second review: Faithful and true; no prior proof found.

oeis-a128828.note: The disproof of Priluck's n == 2 (mod 3) hexagon formula is sound. The model (first construction: lines at integer offsets -m..m except 0, integral apothem and center) gives 1,2,15,28,65,120, matching the data, and agrees with all three of Priluck's formulas for n<=14. With offset 0 allowed it gives Priluck's second-construction count (n+1)^3, an independent check. At n=15, 16, 17 all classes fail, and a(17)=4734 against the formula's 4950. A period-3 quartic has 15 free coefficients, so the formulas just interpolate n=0..14. Priluck's paper calls them conjectures. Second review: Valid disproof: Priluck's quartic formula fails (first at n=15 overall; the formalized n=2 mod 3 branch at n=17). Robust: the true count grows cubically. No earlier report of the failure found.

oeis-a131607.note: a(n)=floor(A001333(n)/10), with the g.f. stated from index 0 (terms 0 for n<4, matching the x^4 factor) and the recurrence for n>12. Checked to n=80 against the data. The proof is the standard argument that A001333 mod 10 has period 12, so it is routine. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful, true, routine periodicity argument. No prior proof found.

oeis-a135231.note: The triple product A103451 * signed A000012 * Pascal and the row sums reproduce the data. Wu's recurrence (n>3), the g.f. and Mathar's a(n)=A001045(n+1)+1 follow from 3a(n)=3+2^(n+1)+(-1)^n (n>=1), checked to 30. Routine, and no prior proof was found. Second review: Faithful, true, a short closed-form computation. No prior proof found.

oeis-a214385.note: Barker's g.f. 2x(4+19x-17x^2+4x^3)/(1-x)^7 and the order-7 recurrence for the 3-row triangular 0..n arrays. My brute force of the formal predicate (cells numbered row by row, each upper cell between its sw/se neighbours, no equal horizontal neighbours) gives 8, 94, 456, 1506, 3976, 9044, which matches the data. Parent A214384 has no proof, and I found none elsewhere. The proof is a finite pattern count by rank decomposition, giving a degree-6 polynomial. Second review: Faithful and true for all n (exact pattern-sum polynomial). Routine finite enumeration. No prior proof found.

oeis-a214449.note: This is a disproof of Kimberling's conjecture that A214449 is A118168 with its first two 1s deleted. The offsets are right: A214449 has offset 1 and A118168 has offset 0, so the claim is A214449(n) = A118168(n+1). I confirmed the counterexample: 158^158 < 188! <= 159^159 gives A214449(188) = 159, while 189! is closer to 158^158 than to 159^159, so A118168(189) = 158. Further failures occur at n = 248, 271 and 310. A118168 lists only about 27 terms, and I found no earlier report of the failure. The disproof is a direct numerical check. Second review: Valid disproof by an exact finite check at n=188 (also fails at 248, 271). A118168 has no b-file and the failure is not noted anywhere I found.

oeis-a214944.note: Barker's g.f. and recurrence for squarefree words of length 5 over n+1 letters. The formal definition (no factor uu with u nonempty, words over Fin(n+1)) reproduces the data with the right offset: a(1) = 0 for binary, then a(2), a(3), ... Lean's extra a(0) = 0 is harmless. Parent A214943 (Shur's growth-rate results) has no proof of the row polynomials. A fixed-length count is a finite sum over squarefree patterns times falling factorials, so the proof is routine. Second review: Faithful and true for all n (exact pattern-sum polynomial). Routine finite enumeration. No prior proof found.

oeis-a215095.note: Scambler's g.f. (x+2x^2)/(1-x-x^2-x^3-2x^4) for the greedy Jacobsthal-sum sequence. The statement's greedy definition reproduces the data, and I checked that it equals the g.f. series for 80 terms. I found no prior proof. The proof locates each greedy step between consecutive Jacobsthal numbers, an elementary induction. Second review: Faithful and true; inductive argument on the greedy rule. No prior proof found.

oeis-a217866.note: The conjecture says the last n in A217865 (first differences of floor(k log k)) comes before the first n+2. As formalized, every index with value n is below every index with value n+2, which is faithful. The proof is elementary: each difference lies strictly within 1 of D(k) = f(k+1)-f(k), and D is increasing by convexity of x log x. I found no prior proof. Short, but not definitional. Second review: Faithful and true via a short monotonicity argument. Same statement as oeis-a217976 (A217976 carries the same conjecture); A217866 is the earlier of the two, so A217976 should not be counted as a separate solve.

oeis-a220018.note: Barker's a(n) = 8n^2-14n-1 (n>2) and the order-3 recurrence for the number of cyclotomic cosets of 3 mod 10^n. The formal orbit-minimum count matches the definition. I checked the data both by brute force (n <= 5) and by the orbit formula Sum_{d|10^n} phi(d)/ord_d(3), which gives the formula for n = 3..39. I found no published proof; a web search found only the conjectures. The proof is a genuine orbit count using orders of 3 modulo 2^a 5^b. Second review: Faithful, true, routine multiplicative-order computation. No prior proof found.

oeis-a220019.note: Barker's a(n) = 5(16n^2-60n+37) for n>3 and the order-3 recurrence for n>6, for the number of cyclotomic cosets of 7 mod 10^n. The statement counts orbits of the cyclic group generated by 7 acting on ZMod(10^n), which is faithful. The orbit formula reproduces the data, matches brute force for n <= 5, and gives the formula for n = 4..39. I found no prior proof. The proof counts orbits via orders of 7 modulo 2^a 5^b. Second review: Faithful, true, routine multiplicative-order computation. No prior proof found.

oeis-a220020.note: Barker's closed form 4(4n^2-7n-1) (n>2), the recurrence (n>5) and the g.f. 2x(8x^4-13x^3-7x^2-x-3)/(x-1)^3 for cyclotomic cosets of 9 mod 10^n. The orbit-quotient definition is faithful and reproduces 6,20,56,140,256 (brute force). The orbit formula confirms the closed form for n = 3..39. I found no prior proof. The proof shares its orbit-counting library with the A220019/A221855 solves, but it covers a different statement. Second review: Faithful, true, routine multiplicative-order computation. No prior proof found.

oeis-a221855.note: Barker's a(n) = 2n(4n-7) (n>2), the recurrence and the g.f. for cyclotomic cosets of 13 mod 10^n. oeis-a252834.note: The n X 6 arrays (within 2, no corner condition; upper-left 0; steps right, down and se add 0 or 1) are formalised faithfully, with Barker's g.f. and the recurrence threshold copied from the entry. Second review: Faithful formalization of Barker's conjecture for column of A252836. The closest prior work (Hardinian arrays, Spahn & Dougherty-Bliss 2024 transfer-matrix note) covers only the corner-and-within variant, and its method would extend here, so the result is routine (lower-triangular transfer matrix, eventually polynomial).

Second review: Short explicit argument: (2n+1)^2 is itself a square, so it first appears as an odd number inside the block of k^2 with k = 2n^2+2n+1, at position (2n^2+2n+1)(3n^2+3n+1) = A068722(n). Faithful, no prior proof found; routine.

oeis-a257106.note: Curtz's two period-3 conjectures on the denominators of the inverse binomial transform of Bernoulli numbers with B(1)=2/3 are stated faithfully, and the definition reproduces the data. My check covers n < 120. By the entry's formula c(n) = B_n - (-1)^n n/6, both claims reduce to von Staudt-Clausen at the prime 3. Routine; no prior proof found. Second review: Follows quickly from the entry's own formula plus von Staudt-Clausen (3-part of the denominator cancels exactly when n=2 mod 3). Routine.

oeis-a259056.note: Wolfdieter Lang's conjecture a(2m-1) = (-1)^(m-1) A034976(m) = (-1)^(m-1) 8^(m-1) m!. The proof evaluates the determinant via a symmetric/antisymmetric block split. No prior proof found. Second review: Determinant evaluation for all odd sizes; faithful and apparently new. Not a finite check (general column-operation argument).

oeis-a259057.note: The conjecture that A259057 is integral (3 | det B_{2m}) is stated faithfully with the same matrix as A259056. I checked divisibility for m <= 11. oeis-a259226.note: Disproof of Seidov's 'strong conjecture' that A259226 (keyword fini,full) ends at a(99)=9867. n = 10538 is a further term: prime(10538) = 111031, s^2 - 111031 is composite for 334 <= s <= 497, so A157480 = A259232 = 136973. oeis-a261594.note: Hanna's mod-3 conjecture. 9*A005836+{0,1,3,4} is just A005836, and mod 3 the series is 1/(1+x), whose square root is prod(1+x^(3^i)), so the proof is short. Caveat: the statement assumes an integer square root A exists rather than proving it (vacuous otherwise). I checked integrality and the residue pattern for n < 120, and A135756 asserts integrality. No prior proof found; routine. Second review: Short argument: 2^(k(k-1)) = 1 mod 3 gives F = 1/(1-2x) mod 3, whose square root is prod (1+x^(3^k)). Routine.

oeis-a172434.note: Bala's Aug 2026 conjecture: a(np^k) == a(np^(k-1)) mod p^(3k) for p >= 5, and the same for the negative extension a(-n) = Sum C(-n,k)^4 Sum C(k,j)^4. The statement is faithful: Ring.choose(-n,k) is the generalized binomial, and aneg reproduces Bala's values 1, 3, 1491, 1663491. I checked both claims numerically for p = 5..13, k = 1,2. I found no prior proof. The cube analogue in A141057 (Bala 2022) is still listed as a conjecture. The proof is a genuine Jacobsthal-Kazandzidis p-adic argument. Second review: Faithful formalization of both of Bala's claims; the fourth-power case is a direct analog of the A141057 result proved in arXiv:2608.11941 with the same technique, so the novelty is modest, but neither claim of A172434 (nor the negative extension) is settled anywhere I could find.

oeis-a175625.note: McEachen's 2023 conjecture says prime terms p of A175625 have p-1 squarefree. It is disproved by p = 106106334883 = 2*3*113*131*1093^2 + 1, built from the Wieferich prime 1093. I checked numerically that p is prime and that p mod 6 = 1, 2^(p-1) = 1 mod p and 2^(p-3) = 1 mod (p-1)/2. No prime in the 10000-term b-file is a counterexample, and the number appears nowhere online. The formalization of the membership test is faithful. Second review: Disproof: the counterexample k = 2*3*113*131*1093^2+1 checks out exactly; the mechanism (ord_{1093^2}(2)=ord_1093(2)) is a real reason the conjecture fails, not a formalization artifact.

oeis-a177258.note: This is Mathar's 2022 conjectured recurrence a(n) = (n-1)(a(n-1)+a(n-2)+a(n-3)) + a(n-4) for derangements with no adjacent transposition. The definition by permutations of Fin n is faithful: I brute-forced it to n = 7 and it matches the data. The recurrence holds to n = 60 by the entry's double sum. Brualdi-Deutsch give recurrences only for a single cycle length q, not this mixed case, and I found it in none of the Fried or Blanco Gomez collections. It is a D-finite derivation from an explicit sum, so routine. Second review: Faithful; routine D-finite recurrence, apparently first proof.

oeis-a178536.note: Granvik's 2021 conjecture is that the first column of the inverse of A178534 is Sum_{d|n} mu(n/d)([d=1]-[2|d]), which equals mu(n) except a(2) = -2. It is stated faithfully via the defining system Sum T(n,k)a(k) = [n=1]. I checked it to n = 120. It follows from the factorization T = A129713*A051731 (the column g.f. of A178534): the Toeplitz inverse of (1-z^2)/(1-z-z^2) has first column [n=1]-[2|n], and the Mobius matrix inverts A051731. I found no written proof, but the argument is routine. Second review: Faithful. The conjecture is a short consequence of Howroyd's (unproved on OEIS) formula in A178534, which the proof establishes; nothing on OEIS marks either as proved.

oeis-a180486.note: Barker's 2019 conjectures (g.f. x(5-2x)/(1-x)^2, a(n) = 2a(n-1) - a(n-2), a(n) = 3n+2) are stated faithfully as the increasing listing of the set of ceilings. A179896(k) = 3k(k-1)/2, which is divisible by k exactly when k is odd. So the set is {(3k-2)/2 : k even >= 4} = {5, 8, 11, ...}. This is elementary and routine, and I found no prior written proof. Second review: Faithful; the Barker formulas follow from a two-line computation (only even nonprimes contribute).

oeis-a182532.note: Coman's four conjectures say Carmichael C with 7*17 | C and last digit 1, 5, 3, 9 is 119(120n+r) with r = 119, 95, 47, 71. Second review: Faithful; true by a one-line Korselt argument (the entry's own program uses C == 825265 mod 5712), so this is a routine, near-folklore result.

oeis-a135571.note: Layman's conjecture is stated faithfully: it counts pairs 1 <= j < i with T(i) - T(j) = n, so only positive triangular numbers are used. The proof is the classical count: representations with j >= 0 correspond to the odd divisors of n (Verhoeff's trapezoid count, cited in the entry), and you subtract 1 when n is triangular. The odd part of n is a square iff n is a square or twice a square, and twice a square is never triangular. I checked the equivalence numerically for n < 1500 and found no earlier write-up of this exact corollary, so it is routine but new. Second review: Faithful. The proof is the classical odd-divisor count of Verhoeff (j>=0) minus 1 when n is triangular, plus the fact that k(k+1)=4m^2 is impossible. A short argument from facts in the entry; no earlier write-up of this corollary found.

oeis-a140254.note: The conjectures (mu(n) = 0 gives a(n) = 0, mu = 1 gives a negative value for n > 1, mu = -1 gives a positive value, and mu(n) = -a(n)/|a(n)|) are stated faithfully, with A014963 equal to the least prime for prime powers and 1 otherwise, offset 1. The proof shows a(n) = -mu(n) * Sum_{p|n} (p-1) for n > 1, an elementary multiplicative computation. I checked it numerically for n < 3000. No earlier proof was found in the entry, its cross-references, the Lean libraries or the OEIS proof collections. Second review: Faithful formalization of Adamson/Granvik's sign conjectures. They follow from a(n) = -mu(n)*sum_{p|n}(p-1) for n>1, an elementary multiplicative computation. No prior proof found.

oeis-a158495.note: Mathar's recurrence for the coefficients of ((1-4x) + sqrt(1-4x))/(2(1-2x)) is stated for n >= 3. It genuinely fails at n = 2 (the LHS is 4), and Mathar gives no range, so starting at 3 is the right reading. The proof is a routine algebraic-g.f. computation. The sister entry A126966 carries the same D-finite recurrence, and since a(n) = (2*0^n - 2^n + A126966(n))/2 with 2^n annihilated by the operator, the result follows. Routine. Second review: Faithful corrected form (Mathar's recurrence holds for n>=3, fails at n=2). Routine: it is essentially the stated recurrence of A126966 transferred through the entry's own formula, so any announcement should say this is a near-immediate corollary and that the conjecture as printed is false at n=2.

oeis-a159864.note: Mathar's row-sum conjecture, with the upper limits as corrected on 2026-11-24, is stated faithfully: T(n,k) = k-th forward difference of F at n-k. It is elementary: Delta F(i) = F(i-1), so T(n,k) = F(n-2k) (Somos's 2022 program in the entry). The even rows then cancel by F(-m) = (-1)^(m+1) F(m), and the odd rows sum to 2F(2n+2). Correct but routine. Second review: Faithful to the corrected conjecture (the correction only fixes the summation limits to the full rows). Routine from Heinz's closed form in the entry.

oeis-a162475.note: Mathar's recurrence for the coefficients of c(x/(1-x)^4) is stated for n >= 6. The g.f. is pinned down by T^2(1-x)^4 = (1-x)^4 - 4x with T(0) = 1. I checked it numerically for n < 60. A routine algebraic-g.f. certificate. Second review: Faithful corrected form (holds for n>=6, false at n=5 as printed). Routine D-finite recurrence; no prior proof found. Announcement should state the n=5 exception.

oeis-a164010.note: Mathar's conjecture a(n) = n(n+9) for n > 16 is stated faithfully. Row 10 of A163280 is the 10th smallest j with largest divisor <= sqrt(j) equal to n, the offset-0 padding matches the data, and the array reproduces the terms 23, 46, 57, ... I checked it for 17 <= n < 400. It is elementary: the candidates are n*m with m in [n, n+9], and a divisor n+i in (n, sqrt(n*m)] would have to divide i(m-n-i) <= 20, which is impossible for n > 16. Routine. Second review: Faithful. The ten smallest j are k*k..k*(k+9) once k+j > j(i-j) for all small i, j, i.e. k>16; a short divisor argument. Routine; no prior proof found.

oeis-a280739.note: Valianatos's conjecture that a(n) exists for all n>=4. The sInf recursion (0 on empty set) is faithful and a(4)=4. The proof is the elementary bound c^3 <= 3^sopfr(c) (from p^3 <= 3^p), so a(n-1) < 9*3^k, 4*3^k or 6*3^k, which have sopfr n. Not vacuous but easy; no prior proof found. Routine. Second review: The statement is faithful, and the conjecture is true by a three-line monotonicity argument (the maximal product with prime-sum n exceeds every number with prime-sum n-1). No earlier proof found anywhere. The easiness is real but does not make the statement vacuous. Routine.

The paper (and their 2023-2025 follow-ups I checked) only conjecture the limit; it follows since b_k = tan(pi/2^(k+2)) (the paper's eq. 2), so c_k = tan(pi/4 - pi/2^(k+2)). The conjecture is true and follows in a few lines from the half-angle identity that the source paper itself states as its equation (2). No one published that step, so it is new but routine. The easiness does not make the formal statement vacuous.

oeis-a227776.note: Kimberling's conjecture that 6n^2+1 is the least splitter of s(n) = n sin(1/n) and s(n+1) is stated faithfully for n >= 1, with splitter as defined in A227631, and the example lists 6/7, 24/25, .... The proof uses the Taylor bounds 1 - 1/(6m^2) < s(m) < 1: c/d = 6n^2/(6n^2+1) splits, and any c/d < 1 with d <= 6n^2 lies below s(n). It is elementary. No prior proof found. Second review: Kimberling's least-splitter conjecture for n sin(1/n). It follows by a short Taylor-bound argument. Faithful, and no prior proof was found in the A2276xx splitter family or on the web.

oeis-a228212.note: Barker's a(n) = 3^(n+2) - 2^(n+2) for n > 3, counting distinct second-difference arrays of 0..2 arrays of length n+2. It is stated faithfully (a(4) = 665 matches; a(3) = 199 is not 211, so the threshold is right). Two arrays have the same second differences iff they differ by an integer linear function, and once n+1 > 2k only constant shifts are possible. So each class has exactly one member containing a 0. The proof is this elementary argument. The parent A228218 has no proof. Second review: Barker's closed form for a Hardin difference-array count. The definition reproduces the data, and the formula holds exactly where it is stated. Finite-state count, so routine.

oeis-a228214.note: This is the same family as A228212, for k = 4: a(n) = 5^(n+2) - 4^(n+2) for n > 7. The statement is faithful, and a(8) = 8717049 matches the data. Since n+1 > 2k, the linear part of any difference is forced to be 0, so classes correspond to arrays containing a 0. Elementary; no prior proof found in A228218. Second review: Barker's closed form for a Hardin difference-array count. The definition reproduces the data, and the formula holds exactly where it is stated. Finite-state count, so routine.

oeis-a228219.note: Barker's g.f. x(15+4x+x^2)/(1-x)^3 and order-3 recurrence for n > 3, i.e. a(n) = 10n^2+4n+1, the number of second-difference pairs of length-4 arrays over 0..n. The a(0) slot is zeroed in the g.f. as the offset requires. The proof characterizes the image as the lattice points of an octagon and counts them. I brute-forced n <= 8 and all agree. Elementary. Second review: A quadratic count; routine. Faithful, and no prior proof was found.

oeis-a230113.note: Barker's recurrence (n > 17) and g.f. for Croft's digital-root sequence. The statement's definition, dr(dr F(m) + dr L(m-1)) with m running over the numbers prime to 30, follows the entry's example (A227896 starts at F(1), A233766 at L(0)) and reproduces all 68 data terms. oeis-a230218.note: Hanna's parity conjecture: for n > 0, a(n) is odd iff n is a power of 2. The recursive definition, a(n) = -[x^n](earlier part)^(n^2+n+1)/(n^2+n+1) with a(0) = a(1) = 1, reproduces the data, and I checked that the division is exact and the parity claim holds for n < 70. The proof shows that the division is exact and that mod 2 the series is B with B = B^2 + X. That is a short but genuine argument. No prior proof found in the sister entries (A229044 lists the analogous claim, still as a conjecture). Second review: A genuine proof. Mod 2 the g.f. is B = 1 + sum x^(2^k), the solution of B = B^2 + X, using that n^2+n+1 is odd. Web search (Hanna parity, A292877 cross-reference, Fried's parity papers) found no prior proof. Faithful.

oeis-a233419.note: Greathouse's conjecture that every k not divisible by 4 divides infinitely many odious numbers of order 2, A000069(A000069(j)). It is stated faithfully: odious(j) = 2(j-1) + [weight(j-1) even] gives A000069, and secondOdious reproduces A232637. I checked numerically that every k < 400 with 4 not dividing k has a multiple among the first 2*10^5 terms. The proof is a genuine binary-block (Thue-Morse) construction. No prior proof found; trureturing has EvilOdious material but nothing on A232637 or A233419. Second review: A new proof of Greathouse's conjecture. Web search, including Allouche-Shallit 'Beyond odious and evil', found no prior proof. Faithful.

oeis-a234269.note: Mathar's D-finite recurrence for the g.f. (1-2x^2-S)/(2xS), S = sqrt(1-4x^2-4x^3), for n >= 4. The coefficients expand Mathar's factored form exactly, and S and G are uniquely determined by the hypotheses. I checked the recurrence against the expansion for n < 40, and the expansion matches the data. Routine elimination to an ODE. Second review: Mathar's holonomic recurrence for an algebraic g.f.; routine and faithful. Not among the 33 Ekhad-Yang-Zeilberger proofs.

oeis-a238714.note: Stauduhar's conjecture that the set of final divisors of the rem -> rem mod sopfr(rem) loop is exactly {m >= 2, m != 6}. The loop matches A238529's SageMath and PARI programs, and the model reproduces the data. The proof is elementary: sopfr(r) = 6 forces r in {8, 9}, where the loop continues; m is attained via r = m*u with sopfr(u) = m - sopfr(m). No prior proof found. Second review: A short constructive argument; routine. Faithful, and no prior proof was found.

oeis-a283754.note: Israel's 2a(n+1)-a(n) = 3^n*A055620(n) is stated faithfully, A055620 being characterized as the digits of the 6-adic idempotent with first digit 4 (unique). It is a short CRT argument: E_n = E mod 6^n is 0 mod 2^n and 1 mod 3^n, so E_n = 2^n a(n), and the identity is (E_{n+1}-E_n)/2^n. Kenny Lau's 2018 program in A055620 already computes the digits as a(n)*2^n, but no proof is written. Verified for n<59. No prior proof found (OEIS entry and cross-references, trureturing, thatnealpatel/proofs, Palomar, Epoch, Blanco Gómez/Fried, formal-conjectures, conjectures.io). Second review: Faithful and true. It is a two-line CRT argument: e mod 6^n is the residue that is 0 mod 2^n and 1 mod 3^n, which is 2^n*a(n), so digit n is (2^(n+1)a(n+1)-2^n a(n))/6^n. A055620's own PROG line already computes the idempotent this way, so the result is close to folklore. No explicit prior proof was found.

oeis-a284691.note: Masad's Conjecture 1 (every (10^c-1)*A074992(i)*A074992(j), c>=1, is a base-10 palindrome) is stated faithfully; Conjecture 2 is too vague and is rightly left out. The proof writes the number as a sum of 9 runs of c ones, so every digit is at most 9 (no carries) and the coefficients are symmetric. I checked all c<70, i,j<35. No prior proof found (OEIS entry and cross-references, trureturing, thatnealpatel/proofs, Palomar, Epoch, Blanco Gómez/Fried, formal-conjectures, conjectures.io). Second review: Faithful and true. 9*A(i)*A(j) = (1+x^i+x^2i)(1+x^j+x^2j) at x=10, and times the repunit R_c the coefficients are at most 9, so there are no carries and the palindromic polynomial gives a palindromic number. Short argument, routine. No prior proof found.

oeis-a285052.note: The conjecture a(n) = 4^omega(n) is stated faithfully (each residue mapped to the idempotent among its positive powers, which is unique in a finite ring; ordered triples (e(a),e(b),e(ab))). oeis-a293136.note: Arndt's conjecture is stated faithfully: the last nonzero k in row n is A293137(n) = floor(2 sqrt n)-1 (Nat.sqrt(4n)-1), with row 0 = [1]. Second review: Faithful and true. mo-205907.note: Exact answer: a polynomial of degree <= d with f(0)=0 and f in [1-a/2,1+a/2] on [1-a,1+a] exists iff d >= ceil(arcosh(2/a)/arcosh(1/a)). This is the classical Chebyshev extremal property: min max |1-f| = 1/T_d(1/a), so we need T_d(1/a) >= 2/a. Faithful, and checked by hand at a=1/2 (d=2). The MO question has no answers. It is a textbook consequence, so routine. Second review: Faithful and correct. The answer is a direct corollary of the classical Chebyshev extremal growth bound (the question title even names Chebyshev). Not settled on MO.

mo-217457.note: I checked the recurrences index by index against the question: seq(n+3) uses s_1..s_{n+2}, the force terms are -a_{n-2} and -a_{n-2}c_0 + c_0 sum a_k b_{n-1-k}, and alpha_2, beta_2 match. The hypotheses are a joint PMF (arbitrary dependence, as the asker allowed) and 0<s_0<1. The statement covers both D_{n+1}>D_n>0 and the tilde-D claim. The proof is a ~1000-line random-walk / substochastic-matrix argument. No MO answer, and the source paper (Grigutis–Korvel–Šiaulys, arXiv:1601.01153) defines alpha, beta but does not prove the determinant property. Non-routine. Second review: Disproof valid within the stated hypotheses. The Lean counterexample is a degenerate equality case (two claims identically zero). The claim also fails strictly for dependent laws, so the negative answer is robust. The proof file also proves weak monotonicity for independent claims.

mo-290383.note: Disproof by M = I_2 (rank 2, r=1). If I = P - Q with P, Q nonnegative of rank <= 1, then det Q = 0 and det P = det(I+Q) = 1 + tr Q >= 1, so P has rank 2. Faithful to the question (rational nonnegative M of rank 2r, nonnegative rational parts of rank <= r). Unanswered on MO but elementary, so routine. Second review: Valid, very short counterexample (the 2x2 identity) to the question as asked. Nobody had pointed this out on MO.

mo-319396.note: Answer: mu([-1,1]) = mu{0} + sum_j sum_i (-1)^i C(j,i) m_{2i+2}, from sum_j x^2(1-x^2)^j = 1 for 0<|x|<=1. So finiteness is decided by the atom at 0 plus that moment series. delta_0 vs infinity*delta_0 have identical positive moments, answering the edit's question. Correct and faithful (positive Borel measures on [-1,1], moments n >= 1). Elementary, so routine. Second review: Faithful and correct. The answer (no condition from moments alone, because of the atom at 0; otherwise an explicit series) is short and elementary. The second conjunct relies on an infinite atom at 0, which the asker's framework allows (they use non-locally-finite densities).

mo-335694.note: Seva Lev's question asks whether pairs (f,m), 2 <= m <= deg f/2, other than f = c(x-a)^d + r with deg r < m admit a non-constant Q with (Qf)^{(k)} = P_k f + R_k, deg R_k < m, for 1 <= k <= deg Q. It drops the optional relaxed variants (k up to deg Q/2 or k<=100), but those were only an extra wish.

mo-364129.note: The statement matches the question: v in Q^(N-1) (as v on ZMod N with v 0 = 0) lies in the kernel of M_Gamma = (zeta^(nir) - zeta^(ni)) exactly when v is constant on Gamma-orbits. Exponents are taken via ZMod.val, which is harmless since zeta^N = 1. The question has 0 answers and no settling comments. The result is a direct discrete-Fourier argument: the conditions say the transform of v is Gamma-invariant on nonzero frequencies, and Fourier inversion moves this invariance to v. Second review: Correct and faithful. The answer is an immediate discrete-Fourier-inversion argument, so it is routine.

mo-387067.note: The statement transcribes the first (real-rank) question with blowUp built faithfully (identity for +1, anti-identity for -1) and O(r) with constants depending on m. The only answer (2021) proved rank f(M) = ceil(m/2) rank|M| + floor(m/2) rank M but left open whether rank|M| = O(rank M) for {0,+-1} matrices. The disproof settles this. On the r x r grid it takes M = B - D (B, D record equal first and second coordinates): rank M <= 2r, while |M| = B + D - 2I has rank about r^2, so with m = 2 the rank of f(M) is not O(rank M). It is a short Kronecker-product construction. Second review: Valid disproof (answer No) that completes the partial MO answer with an explicit {0,+-1} family where rank|M| is quadratic in rank M. Fidelity is fine.

mo-400876.note: The statement is faithful: a factor is (1-t)P + tQ with P, Q permutation matrices and t in [0,1]; products form the generated submonoid; it claims an open neighbourhood of N_n whose doubly stochastic members are all such products, for every n >= 1. The question has 0 answers. Van Name's linked answers only factor N_n itself and prove that F_n lies in the closure of its interior, which does not give N_n in the interior (N_n is singular, so his inverse-function argument does not apply there). The 877-line proof builds a local surjectivity argument at the rank-one point. It is a port of @connoranderson's own earlier site proof, which is credited in the header. Second review: Faithful; affirmative answer. No prior solution found in gossip/consensus literature searches.

mo-421810.note: The statement is faithful: G on n+1 labelled vertices, G-i is the principal submatrix deleting row and column i, and a common complex root of phi'(G) and phi'(G-i) is a root of phi(G). The question has 0 answers or comments. The proof differentiates P adj(P) = f I to get Q^2 + fQ' = f'Q. At a common critical point the i-th diagonal entry gives sum_j Q_ij^2 = 0, so row i of the adjugate vanishes and f = 0; real-rootedness comes from Rolle and the spectral theorem. This is essentially Godsil's walk-generating identity phi(G-i)phi'(G) - phi'(G-i)phi(G) = sum_j phi_ij^2, so it is a short consequence of a standard identity. Second review: Correct, short argument from a standard Christoffel-Darboux-type identity (the statement implicitly answers Yes). Not found as a stated result.

mo-472069.note: The statement is faithful: A generates G, A^2 is a union of left H-cosets, H is inclusion-maximal with this property among overgroups, |A^2| < 2|A|, and the claim is that H is normal. The disproof is in D_5 with A = {r1, r4, sr1, sr4} and H = {1, sr0}. I checked it independently: |A^2| = 6 < 8, A^2 is H-right-invariant, the only proper overgroup is D_5 itself, and H is not normal. The question has 0 answers, and its comments only note AA^-1 = A^-1A and Tao's lemma. It is a small explicit counterexample. Second review: Valid small counterexample; the OP expected a simple one to exist. Finite check.

mo-478522.note: The statement is faithful: C symmetric positive definite with entries in [0,1] and unit diagonal, f(x) = sum_i x_i log((Cx)_i), and the claim that f is convex on the open simplex. The disproof uses C = [[1,0,5/8],[0,1,3/4],[5/8,3/4,1]] (det 3/64 > 0) and a midpoint violation at x = (1/5,1/5,3/5), y = (2/5,2/5,1/5). I confirmed numerically that f is not midpoint-convex for this C. The question has 0 answers. One comment splits f into convex and concave parts without deciding, and the asker's 'my conjecture is incorrect' reply was walked back by the commenter ('Not necessarily'). It is a single explicit counterexample. Second review: Valid explicit counterexample; numerically confirmed.

mo-503562.note: The statement matches the asker's first request: for an injective union-closed family covering [q], det M = P * prod_k x_k^{f(k)} with no x_k dividing P. The proof factors prod_{k in A_i} x_k from row i (giving the exponent f(k), as one comment noted) and shows that the remaining matrix has constant term det[A_j subset A_i] = 1 (unitriangular), so P has constant coefficient 1. The question has 0 answers; the only comment gives the lower bound. Short and elementary; it does not even need union-closure. The 'interpretation of P' part is not formalised. Second review: Correct and faithful for the exponent claim. The argument is short (constant term 1) and also follows from the Lindstrom-Wilf determinant the asker cites.

mse-2172922.note: The statement (for every eps > 0 there are infinitely many N with frac(sum_{n=2}^N log n) < eps) is faithful. The question has 0 answers. Ofir's answer to the linked question only explains the 'parabolas' heuristically: increments are nearly integers when n is near e^k. The proof makes this rigorous. For n in [e^(m+delta), e^(m+2delta)), f(i) = logSum(N+i) - m i rises by steps in [delta, 2delta), so it crosses an integer with small fractional part. Correct and elementary. Second review: Faithful; the elementary 'small fractional steps near e^k' argument settles density of {log N!} near 0. No prior solution found.

mse-886041.note: The statement is faithful: beta(n,k) is the largest d <= k dividing n, S(k) = sum_{n<=k!} beta(n,k), T(k) = #{ij : i <= k, j <= k!}, and also the lcm(1..k) variant, for every k >= 1. I checked S = T numerically for k <= 8 (matching A126959: 1,3,12,58,352,... and A101459: 1,3,12,29,176,...).
