The proof is short: x <= km is in the table iff x <= beta(x,k) m, and beta is m-periodic. Second review: Identity true for every k; short periodicity argument. The asker's own 'fails' comment is wrong.

opg-outward-reloid-of-composition-vs-com.note: The statement is faithful: funcoid composition is X[g o f]Z iff <f>X meets <g^-1>Z, (RLD)_out f is the filter generated by up f, reloid composition is generated by the G o F, and Mathlib's filter order is Porton's order. It is still listed as Conjecture 1356 in Porton's current book. The disproof takes f = Omega x^FCD {pt} and g = {pt} x^FCD Omega. Then (RLD)_out g o (RLD)_out f = Omega x^RLD Omega, while (RLD)_out(g o f) = (RLD)_out(Omega x^FCD Omega) contains the off-diagonal. This is a short consequence of Porton's own observation that the 'second product' (RLD)_out(A x^FCD B) can be strictly below A x^RLD B (book Examples 1368/1370), though he never connected the two. Second review: The disproof is valid given Porton's definitions as encoded (I checked each against what I know of Algebraic General Topology). Residual risk: I could not open the book to confirm (RLD)out = meet of up f verbatim. The counterexample is surprisingly simple for a posed conjecture.

oeis-a181674.note: Disproof. Greathouse's 'average order Theta(log log n)' is formalized as summatory count Theta(N log log N), the standard reading. The proof shows along N=2^(2^k) the count is O(N) (O(2^k/k) primorials times O(Nk/2^k) semiprimes via Chebyshev bounds), so the lower bound fails. Heuristically and numerically (N<=2e6, ratio ~1.57) the true average order is constant. No prior refutation found. Second review: Disproof valid (the true average order is Theta(1)); numerics agree.

oeis-a097154.note: Faithful: f(x)=reverse(x)-maxdigit(x) in base 10 (trailing zeros dropped on reversal, as in the entry's 89->98 example), fixed-point set stated as {0,89}. Since reverse(x) is congruent to x mod 9 and maxdigit<=9, a nonzero fixed point needs reverse(x)=x+9, and a digit argument leaves only 89. oeis-a321727.note: Disproof of Sun's conjecture a(n)>0. Faithful: prime(k)=Nat.nth Nat.Prime on Fin n, f a permutation, prime(k)+prime(f(k))+1 prime for all k. The Lean proof shows a prime = 1 mod 3 can only be paired with 3 or a prime = 2 mod 3, so a permutation needs #(1 mod 3) <= #(2 mod 3)+1 among the first n primes, and then certifies by a formal Meissel-type count that this fails near x=608981813029 (the Bays-Hudson first Chebyshev-bias reversal for modulus 3). The MO question 315581 cited by the entry is now deleted (404) and no public refutation was found (entry, sister entries A321597/A321610/A321611, Palomar, Lean lists, web). Non-routine: needs an exact prime count to ~6e11 inside Lean. Second review: Disproof: the mod-3 obstruction plus the first prime-race crossing pi(x;3,1)>pi(x;3,2) at 608981813029 gives a(n)=0 for n=pi(608981813029). The Lean proof certifies the prime counts in-kernel. No earlier refutation was found; the one gap is the deleted MO thread, which is no longer public.

oeis-a322921.note: Disproof. The statement (n>=48 even; among n, n+2, n+4 the multiple of 6 has at least as many unordered two-prime decompositions as each other) is the entry's conjecture in its weak form, so refuting it is at least as strong. oeis-a325498.note: Kimberling's conjecture that every gap of A036668 (greedy: not 2x,3x of an earlier term) lies in {1,2,3,4} is stated faithfully. The recursive 'selected' predicate matches the greedy definition, since a(m) < n whenever 2a(m)=n or 3a(m)=n. My sieve to 3e6 shows exactly the claimed gap set. No prior proof found, but it is immediate because every number coprime to 6 is a term (A036668's name: 2^i 3^j k with i+j even). Routine. Second review: Correct and faithful. It is an elementary consequence of the greedy structure (all numbers coprime to 6 or 12 are members, with a short case check for the complement).

oeis-a325499.note: Kimberling's conjecture that every gap of A325424 (greedy: not 2x,3x of an earlier term) lies in {1,...,7} is stated faithfully. Second review: Correct and faithful. It is an elementary consequence of the greedy structure (all numbers coprime to 6 or 12 are members, with a short case check for the complement).

oeis-a327464.note: Sloane's conjecture (max value 107, first reached at n=883) is stated faithfully as a(n)<=107 for all n, a(883)=107 and a(n)<107 before that. It has the entry's base-5 reversal and next-prime/next-composite definitions. My recomputation to n=2*10^5 gives max 107, first at 883. The proof is a finite reachable-set argument by n mod 6, the method Sigrist and Weimholt used in A326344 and which the base-3 and base-7 sisters A326894/A327241 report adapting. For base 5 no confirmation was recorded in the entry or its sisters. Routine. Second review: Correct: the orbit is eventually confined, so the conjecture reduces to a finite check. No earlier proof was found.

oeis-a327565.note: The conjecture that, for m>2, the first n with a(n)=m is 2^(m-3)+1 is stated faithfully. The state machine matches the entry's example and PARI program, with the initial state counted as seen. The statement header correctly notes that the formula line's A094373(m-1) is an index slip for A094373(m-2), which is the same claim. My simulation for n<70000 reproduces the data and the first occurrences 2,3,5,9,...,65537. No prior proof (entry, sisters A327613/A327614, Palomar, Lean lists). Routine (explicit orbit of 2n - x/2). Second review: Faithful, and the proof is a real (short) orbit analysis. No earlier proof was found.

oeis-a328544.note: Sloane's conjecture that the terms are exactly 0, 5, 6 and the repunits is stated faithfully as a full characterization: dec 0 = [0], substring as List.IsInfix, the condition for every digit d. My search to 3*10^6 gives exactly 0,1,5,6,11,...,1111111. No prior proof found (entry, A328095, Palomar, Lean lists). Routine: digit analysis, a finite check below 1000 plus an argument for longer k. Second review: An easy digit argument, which is correct. No earlier proof was found.

oeis-a329231.note: Disproof of Kagey's C2 (largest n with a(n)=5 is 1972). The procedure is transcribed faithfully: my simulation with the same conventions reproduces all 2048 b-file terms of A329231 (and A329232). It gives a(2436)=5, the counterexample the Lean proof certifies by kernel computation; 2436 lies just past the b-file range. No prior refutation found (entry, MSE 3418970 which has only comments, Palomar). Routine: a finite computation. Second review: Refutes conjecture C2 (largest n with a(n)=5 is 1972) with a(2436)=5, which my own simulation confirms. Only C2 is refuted: C1 (a(n)=1 iff n=3,7,2^k) is untouched, so announce it as 'C2 refuted', not as A329231 settled.

oeis-a329232.note: Kagey's conjecture (no counterclockwise hops before all positions are reached iff n is a power of 2) is stated faithfully and without assuming the procedure stops. The counted hop range was checked against the whole b-file: my simulation with these conventions matches all 2048 terms, and the zero set up to 4096 is exactly the powers of 2. MSE 3418970 has no answer and nothing else settles it. Routine: purely clockwise runs visit the triangular numbers mod n, which cover all residues only for n=2^k. Second review: Faithful and proved for all n. The argument (clockwise-only walk = triangular numbers mod n, which cover Z/n iff n=2^k) is short but not in the entry.

oeis-a330733.note: Hood's two conjectures (right diagonal = A002033(n-1); each prime column with its zeros removed = A002033) are stated faithfully. Proper divisors exclude 1 and n, matching the worked example for 12. The column claim is split into: zero off multiples of p, R(mp,p) = A002033(m-1), and A002033 never 0. A Python re-implementation reproduces row 12, and both claims hold for n<400 and p<=13. No prior proof found. Routine: both sides satisfy the ordered-factorization recursion H(n) = sum over d|n, d<n of H(d). Second review: Correct, a short induction on the defining recursion.

oeis-a331124.note: Disproof of Konig's conjecture that the no-caching evaluation count is eventually <= C*n^(4/3). It is stated in its weakest form (some C>0 and N), so the refutation is strong, and calls(n) matches the entry's recurrence. The Lean proof builds indices k with index(k) <= 8*64^k and calls >= 257^k, so calls/n^(4/3) >= (257/256)^k/16 is unbounded. Numerically, max a(n)/n^(4/3) on [2^k,2^(k+1)) creeps up from 1.177 (k=8) to 1.306 (k=22), so the true exponent is only slightly above 4/3. No prior refutation found. Non-routine: it needed the right self-similar family. Second review: Valid disproof, though only barely: the true growth exponent is about 1.344, slightly above 4/3. Worth saying so when announcing, since König's 'small constant times n^(4/3)' was an empirical estimate.

oeis-a331164.note: Konig's conjecture a(n)=O(log n) for the cached evaluation count is stated as a Big-O over atTop. The count is 1 plus the child lookups of each distinct expanded argument >2, with 0,1,2 pre-cached, and my re-implementation reproduces every listed data term. The proof bounds the arguments at depth d to the band [n/2^d-3, n/2^d+2]. No prior proof found. Routine. Second review: Correct. With caching each recursion depth holds only O(1) distinct arguments, so O(log n) follows by a short argument.

oeis-a334592.note: Kagey's conjecture 'records occur at powers of two' is stated as: n is a strict record (more zeros than every smaller positive m) iff n=2^e, with the XOR triangle and zero count implemented directly. My computation for n<2^15 gives exactly the powers of 2 as strict records. The linked MO 359138 is about rotation-invariant triangles, not records, and no other prior proof was found. Routine: a power of 2 gives T(e) zeros, and any leading-1 triangle of side L+1 has at least L+1 ones, with equality only for 10...0. Second review: Correct and elementary: a row starting with 1 forces at least L ones, and 2^(L-1) attains the bound.

oeis-a334886.note: Bala's conjecture p^2 | numerator of A'(p-1) for primes p>=5 is stated faithfully, with Mathlib harmonic numbers and Rat.num. It is checked for 5<=p<120, and it fails at p=3 as the header notes. Gessel 1982 and Rowland-Yassawi-Krattenthaler (arXiv:2005.04801, Thm 8) only give congruences that imply A'(p-1) = 0 mod p, and no mod p^2 proof was found. The Lean proof is an elementary p-adic computation (e(k)=C(p-1+k,k)/p, sum k^(p-3) = 0 mod p). Routine. Second review: A new elementary proof (C(p-1+k,k)=p*e(k), Lucas, sum of k^(p-3) = 0 mod p). No earlier proof was found in the Apéry literature.

oeis-a335012.note: Eu's conjecture (a(n)=n-1 iff n is a long period prime, with 2 included as in A006883) is stated faithfully. The count of residues of the first n repunits is taken in ZMod n, and n=1 is correctly excluded. My computation for n<6000 shows the equivalence with no exceptions. No prior proof found (entry, Israel's comment relating a(n) to A084680 when gcd(n,30)=1, Palomar, Lean lists). Routine: order-of-10 argument plus handling of the factors 2, 3, 5. Second review: Correct, a short classification via the order of 10 mod n.

oeis-a336759.note: Shapiro's conjecture that A336759 is infinite is stated faithfully. For every n there is a positive m that is a sum of distinct repdigits and every such representation uses at least n of them. No prior proof found (entry, sister A336748, Palomar, Lean lists). Routine counting: the subset sums of L repunits give 2^L representable numbers below 10^(L+1), but sums of fewer than n repdigits of length <= L+1 number only polynomially many in L. Second review: Correct pigeonhole/counting proof.

oeis-a336972.note: Barker's g.f. and order-15 recurrence (n>15) for the sum of the two smallest sides over integer triangles of perimeter n are stated faithfully, with a(n) defined by the entry's own double-sum formula. My computation of the triangle sum satisfies the g.f. identity to n=119. No prior proof found (entry, Palomar, Lean lists). Routine: a quasi-polynomial count. Second review: A routine rational g.f. identity.

oeis-a337500.note: Mathar's conjectured D-finite recurrence is stated faithfully for n>=3. a(n) is the sum of C(n,k) over |n-2k|<=3 (the walks-within-3-of-origin reading in the entry's comments), which reproduces the data. I checked the recurrence for 3<=n<300. Unlike the sister A337499, no verification is recorded in the entry, and nothing else was found. Routine: the closed forms (m+1)a(2m) = (3m+1)C(2m,m) and (m+2)a(2m+1) = 4(2m+1)C(2m,m). Second review: A routine holonomic recurrence for a binomial sum.

oeis-a337945.note: Luschny's conjecture (m is a term iff m*Clausen(m,1) != 2*Clausen(m,0), i.e. iff m is not odd squarefree) is stated faithfully as both equivalences, with A160014 transcribed. My check for m<3000 agrees. No prior proof found (entry, sisters A337101/A337102/A039956, Palomar, Lean lists). Routine: the condition reduces to m | 2s^2 for some 1<=s<=m/2, which fails exactly when m is odd squarefree, and Clausen(m,1)=2 for odd m. Second review: Correct and elementary (m divides 2s^2 forces m | s when m is odd and squarefree).

oeis-a337950.note: Hanna's conjecture a(4n+k) = 0 mod 5 for k=1,2,3 is stated faithfully. A is defined by F*A = -x*F' with F the theta series, which is equivalent to the L.g.f. -log F. My recomputation reproduces the data and the congruence for indices up to 400. No proof in the entry (the analogous mod-3 claim in A337948 is also still open there), Palomar or Lean lists. Routine given the entry's Jacobi-triple-product expansion, since 4 = -1 mod 5. Second review: Routine: for odd n, 4^n+1 = 0 mod 5, so theta mod 5 is a series in x^4, and so is -x theta'/theta.

oeis-a338020.note: Rush's conjecture (for k>=2, consecutive triples are triangle sides and the differences form a degenerate triangle) is stated faithfully, with the radius condition taken strictly as in the entry. The degenerate part reduces to strict monotonicity, x=y+z being an identity. My high-precision computation for k<3000 confirms it. No prior proof found. Nearly trivial but not definitional: the proof uses pi(2n-1)-1 <= a(n) < pi(2n-1)+1. Routine. Second review: Correct and routine.

mo-104812.note: Disproof: an explicit space X (N x Side x R, with a 'Side' topology built from eventual domination of rates) and a maximal ideal K of the sequence ring give two intersections of maximal ideals whose sum excludes the witness, so the sum is not an intersection of maximal ideals. Fidelity is fine: an arbitrary topological space is enough because C(X) is isomorphic to C(Y) for a Tychonoff Y. The question has no answers, and web searches on sums of strongly z-ideals / sz-ideals found no prior counterexample (Azarpanah–Parsinia treat sums of z-ideals only). Non-routine. Second review: A negative answer to an unanswered 2012 MO question, via a Tychonoff counterexample built on a dominance-filter space. The literature search on sz-ideals was reasonable but not exhaustive.

mo-173510.note: Disproof of the quoted conjecture: a1=4, d=13, term 2344 = 8*293 > phi(13)*13^2 = 2028 is composite, and none of the 361 splits 4+13i, 4+13(360-i) is a pair of primes. I rechecked this with sympy, and (4,13) is the first counterexample my search found. The MO question has no answers, and the math.SE cross-post (858764) is deleted. A finite computation, so routine. Second review: Valid finite counterexample, and no earlier refutation was found.

oeis-a362861.note: The statement encodes both sentences of Sun's Conjecture 1(i): the 14 listed n are exactly those for which 2n is not a sum of distinct 5^a+5^b (a Finset of values, so the summands are distinct), and every even number is a sum of distinct 3^a+3^b. I checked numerically up to 2n = 40000 that the exceptions are exactly the listed terms for base 5 and that there are none for base 3. The proof is a verified finite range plus an unbounded extension along geometric rows. I found no prior proof in the entry, the Lean libraries, Zenodo, aiXiv or Palomar. Second review: Faithful to Conjecture 1(i). No prior proof found. Proof uses a standard interval-extension (completeness) argument plus a finite check.

oeis-a362946.note: Lyons's conjecture that only finitely many positive integers are not of the form sum_{i<=k} i^(e_i) with every e_i >= 1 is stated faithfully as Set.Finite. The proof uses exponents 1 and 2 only: raising i's exponent from 1 to 2 adds i(i-1), and subset sums of these steps cover long intervals of each parity. This is elementary. I found no prior proof in the entry (which has no links), the libraries or the proof collections. Second review: Faithful; no prior proof found. Proof: exponents 1 or 2, raising the i-th exponent adds i(i-1), subset sums cover intervals of each parity.

oeis-a363196.note: The statement is faithful: the rightmost 7 is read from Nat.digits, and the claim is a(n) = -1 iff n = 1. n = 1 is ruled out by the period of 3^k mod 100. n = 0, 2, 3 are witnessed by k = 3, 6, 37. For n >= 4 the witness is 3^(3500*10^(n-4)) = 1 + 7*10^n (mod 10^(n+1)), obtained by lifting the exponent. This is elementary, and I found no prior proof. Second review: Faithful. Proof: n=1 via 3^k mod 100; general n via 81^(125*10^k) == 1+10^(k+4) lifting, then 3^(3500*10^k) == 1+7*10^(k+4). No prior proof found.

oeis-a364470.note: The statement matches the entry: a(1) = 1, and a(n) is the least k > a(n-1) with Omega(k(a(n-1)+k)) = n, via sInf. The claim is Israel's a(n+4) = 4a(n) for n >= 7. The proof certifies a(7..11) by decide and then shows that doubling preserves minimality, since odd candidates are too large (3^Omega(k) <= k). This gives a(4t+7) = 32*4^t and the period-4 scaling. The data agree (32, 56, 80, 120, 128, 224, ...). I found no prior proof. Second review: Faithful, no prior proof found; proof bounds Omega via 3^Omega(k)<=k for odd parts.

oeis-a371739.note: I checked the five coefficient polynomials in the Lean statement against R. J. Mathar's OEIS recurrence (Oct 29 2026) as polynomial identities; they agree after expansion. The recurrence holds numerically for n = 4..59. Proving a D-finite recurrence for a binomial partial sum is a routine creative-telescoping exercise. I found no prior proof. Second review: Faithful expansion of Mathar's D-finite recurrence; a creative-telescoping style identity. No prior proof found.

oeis-a373162.note: This is a disproof of Kimberling's complete-monotonicity conjecture, under both readings. The fractions are increasing (x(2) = 5/7 < x(3) = 21/26), so x is not CM. 1 - x(n) = (n+2)/(2(n^2+n+1)) is not CM either. I checked exactly with rationals that (-1)^j Delta^j (1-x)(2) is nonnegative for j < 40 and first fails at j = 40 (about -6.0e-7). This matches the Lean proof, and it is consistent with the complex poles of the rational function. The tsum definition and the CM predicate are faithful, and the j >= 1 alternating reading of 'increasing CM' is the second disjunct. Second review: Disproof is correct under every sensible reading of 'completely monotonic'. Note the duplicate oeis-a373163 (same statement).

oeis-a374105.note: The statement is faithful: if (9^k+3^k+1)/13 is a prime p then k is prime. The proof is the standard cyclotomic argument. 13 | 9^k+3^k+1 iff 3 does not divide k. If k = ab with 1 < a < k and 3 not dividing b, then 9^a+3^a+1 is a proper divisor larger than 13, so the quotient is not prime. This is elementary, like the repunit-prime exponent argument, and I found no specific prior proof for this entry. Second review: Faithful; a standard cyclotomic-factorization argument, not found written for this entry.

oeis-a375852.note: The statement encodes the A309180 coloring as a recursive predicate: i colors n red if n = T^j(i) along a path staying above i. This agrees with the described process, and a simulation to 2*10^5 gives blue = pure numbers. The proof shows that pure numbers have residues in S (impure preimages for 2 mod 3, 4 mod 6, 13 mod 18, essentially Shaw 2006 Thm 2.1) and that blue = positive pure, which gives the union identity. This is elementary, and I found no prior proof of the union claim. Second review: Faithful; the comment follows from Shaw's 2006 theorem (cited in A061641) and the observation that the A309180 coloring's blue numbers are exactly the pure numbers. Routine.

oeis-a376114.note: The statement is faithful: Nat.nth on the two membership predicates, 1-indexed, with A181795 defined by the odd and even divisor counts. The proof shows that m -> 2m is an order-preserving bijection from A376114 onto A181795: for 2^s*u with u odd, the odd divisor count is d(u) and the even count is s*d(u). This is an elementary divisor-count argument, and I found no prior proof. Second review: Faithful, short divisor-count argument. The only related public artifact is an undated trureturing-experiments numerical report without a proof; if a trureturing Lean proof predating 2026-11-28 04:08 UTC appears, re-check.

oeis-a376354.note: The last digit in the greedy triangular-number base is encoded as successive remainders mod T(k) down to T(2) = 3. This reproduces the data (3, 6, 9, 10, 13, ...). The claim is that the set of gaps between consecutive zero-ending positive numbers is exactly {1,2,3}, which I checked numerically to 2*10^5. The proof is elementary (the terminal digit either resets to zero or rises by one, and it is at most 2). I found no prior proof. Second review: Faithful; elementary argument (each step resets the terminal digit to 0 or adds 1, digit <=2).

oeis-a376357.note: The greedy squares-base representation (A007961) is encoded faithfully, and its last digit is the remainder mod 2^2 after the greedy steps. a is Nat.nth of the positions m >= 1 whose last digit is 0. The claim is that the gap set is exactly {1,2,3,4}, which I checked numerically to 3*10^5; the data match (4, 8, 9, 13, ...). The proof is elementary (the last digit is at most 3 and either resets or increments). I found no prior proof. Second review: Faithful; elementary.

oeis-a376639.note: The statement encodes both of Rush's conjectures faithfully, using A151999 (rad phi(k) | k) and A293928 (totients phi(m) with phi(m)^2 = phi(phi(m)m)). The key is the elementary identity phi(t*m) = t*phi(m) when every prime of t divides m. It shows that the m solving phi(m)^2 = phi(phi(m)m) are exactly A151999 (Mathar's 'apparently' remark in A293928). An independent isitsolved paper proved the same claims the same day; by the brief's rule (filing time vs proof commit time) the site commit is 31 minutes earlier, but the PR merged after the iis filing, so precedence is thin. Any announcement should not claim priority over iis:2611.00300.

oeis-a208971.note: Dihedral orbits of 4-tuples in [-n,n] with zero sum and cyclic first and second differences in [-n,n]; this cyclic reading reproduces the data 1,3,4,8,11,18,... (n<=12) and both parity closed forms. (The docstring quotes a different g.f. and date, but main states only the closed forms, which match the entry.) No prior proof found; routine. Second review: Formal statement faithful and true; routine quasi-polynomial count. The header comment misquotes the g.f. and the date and should be fixed before display, but the theorem itself is right.

oeis-a209008.note: Rotation orbits of the same cyclically constrained zero-sum 4-tuples; brute force gives 1,3,5,10,16,26,... = data and both of Barker's parity closed forms for n<=12. No prior proof found; routine. Second review: Faithful (closed forms; omitted g.f. equivalent) and true. Routine. No earlier proof found.

oeis-a209861.note: Karttunen's conjecture A209861(A054429(n)) = A054429(A209861(n)) is stated row by row (row k = [2^k,2^(k+1))) as output(x)+output(rev x) = 3*2^k-1, with A209861(2^k+x) modelled as 2^k + rank of the A209642 tree code of x among row-k codes. That model is not derived in Lean from the A014486 definition, but it reproduces all 89 listed terms of A209861 and 64 of A209642, and the codes of row k are exactly the (2k+2)-bit terms of A209641, so the bridge is sound; the identity itself checks to k=10. No prior proof found; short but non-mechanical rank-reversal argument. Second review: Faithful reformulation and true (checked to 2^16). The proof is a short order-reversal argument on tree codes, so routine. No earlier proof found.

oeis-a213248.note: Nonzero 13th powers in GaloisField 2 n; the entry's unconjectured formula a(n)=M/gcd(M,13) (cyclic unit group) is 12-periodic in its gcd since ord_13(2)=12, which gives Barker's recurrence (n>24) and g.f., both checked against the formula to n=79. Unlike A213243 there is no 'verified' note, so the g.f. was still conjectural; routine. Second review: Faithful and true. It is an immediate consequence of the formula already in the entry (13 | 2^n-1 iff 12 | n), so routine; no earlier written proof of Barker's lines found.

oeis-a214972.note: The L-sieve definition of A152009 (remove first term, delete indices 1,4,7,..., repeat) is encoded via Nat.nth kept and reproduces the A152009 data; the conjecture a(n)=a(n-1)+1 iff n in A152009 checks for all n<27307. No prior proof found (A152009's own floor((3a+3)/2) formula is also only conjectured there). Short but non-mechanical argument (survivor i = i + i/2 + 1). Second review: Faithful and true; the proof is a short structural argument (survivor i -> i+i/2+1), routine. No earlier proof found.

oeis-a218981.note: Statement (infinitely many n=w+x+y+z with all parts positive and sigma(n)=sigma(w)+sigma(x)+sigma(y)+sigma(z)) is faithful to Perry's conjecture. The proof uses the one-line family 5p=p+p+p+2p for primes p>5: sigma(5p)=6(p+1)=3(p+1)+3(p+1). Elementary and near-trivial, but not vacuous; no earlier written proof found (sister A218852 notes a similar twin-prime family only). Second review: Faithful and true. The conjecture is a real 'Conjecture' line but extremely easy (any 5m with gcd(m,10)=1 works), so it is routine and should not be announced as a substantial result.

oeis-a222098.note: Statement (n X 2 arrays over 0..5, steps right and down increase by 0..3 mod 6, top-left 0) is faithful; transfer matrix reproduces 4,46,530,6108,... and the recurrence, g.f. and Binet form to n=26. iis:2611.00233 also proves it but was filed 2026-11-28 04:57 UTC, after the site proof commit (2026-11-27 22:15 UTC); no earlier source found. Routine. Second review: Faithful and true. iis:2611.00233 proved the g.f. and recurrence independently a few hours after the site's proof commit (but before its merge); by commit time the site is first. Routine transfer count.

oeis-a224670.note: Statement counts (n+1) X 3 matrices over 0..2 whose consecutive-row, consecutive-column 2x2 blocks satisfy A^2=A (four integer equations); transfer matrix reproduces 25,50,76,123,... and Barker's g.f., closed form (= -2+20F(n+1)+2(n+1)+(n+1)(n+2)/2) and Hardin's recurrence (n>5) to n=30. The proof reuses the technique of the site's accepted A224671 proof (a different column), not an earlier proof of this entry; no prior proof found. Routine. Second review: Faithful and true; routine transfer-matrix count adapted from the site's own A224671 proof. No outside prior proof found.

oeis-a227512.note: The name's formula is a typo (-1/n + 1/log(...)); the statement uses 1/(log((2n+1)/(2n-1)) - 1/n), which matches the comment, example and data (checked to n=1499 at 60 digits). The closed form 12n^3-floor(9n/5)-1 (all n>=1), the order-8 recurrence (n>=9) and the g.f. all hold numerically. No prior proof found; needs explicit artanh series error bounds, so not purely mechanical. Second review: Faithful and true. The proof is an explicit two-sided bound from the log series (value = 12n^3 - 9n/5 - O(1/n)), short and elementary, so routine. No earlier proof found.

oeis-a338169.note: Faithful: lists of distinct positive integers with maximum n, sum of their sums equals A281912(n) by its first formula. Proof is a reflection x -> n-x argument on subsets of 1..n-1. I recomputed both sides for n = 1..6 (exact agreement). No prior proof found in the entry, A281912 or the proof collections. Second review: Faithful and new as far as searchable. The proof is a short reflection x->n-x counting argument; routine.

oeis-a338635.note: The tail-series encoding of Hanna's continued fraction characterises A uniquely (each tail is forced x-adically), and the true g.f. satisfies it; the statement uses m Fibbinary with m = 0 allowed, which silently fixes the entry's 'A118113(k), k >= 1' (that would wrongly exclude n = 1, where a(1) = 1 is odd). Proof reduces mod 2 to u + u^3 = x and matches the Fibbinary g.f.; I checked parity against the computed series for n < 60. No prior proof found. Second review: Faithful, verified to n=79, no prior proof found. Short but not merely a recurrence check.

oeis-a338722.note: Faithful to A338721 (Heinz's column formula T(n,k) = 2*floor((n-k(k-1)/2)/k) - 1, equivalently the stated one) and A335616's definition. Both sides count the same parametrised consecutive-part partitions; numerically identical with the data for n <= 14. Elementary bookkeeping. Second review: Faithful and true; essentially a g.f. identity (column g.f. x^{T_k}(1+x^k)/((1-x)(1-x^k)) vs Bala's g.f.). The A335616 crossref already asserts it without proof, so 'new' only in the sense of first written proof.

oeis-a340263.note: Statement uses the closed form in the name; it reproduces rows 1-3. Since 2^n is even the polynomial is c1(x-1)^N + c2(x+1)^N, and y = (x+1)/(x-1) turns it into the binomial y^(2^n) + (2^(n+1)-1), irreducible by Capelli (negative constant, not -4b^4). The proof follows that route. No prior proof found (A340312 still calls it '(?)'). Second review: Faithful; a genuine 2021 conjecture with a short Capelli-type proof (the Lean proof does the binomial/Mobius route). No prior proof found.

oeis-a341063.note: Faithful: the totatives in increasing order, the sum over 1-based i+j <= m+1 is the 0-based i+j < m, and the formula is cleared of the /24 in Z. My recomputation gives a(1..12) = 1,1,5,7,35,11,126,70,177,90,715,142 and the formula for all pq with p,q <= 13. The proof is an elementary but real moment computation over units mod pq; no prior proof found. Second review: Faithful, checked numerically, no prior proof found; 517-line algebraic proof.

oeis-a342909.note: The definitions reproduce the 31 listed terms (I recomputed them). The theorem has a(n+1) < n (which the entry says follows from the definition) and Sycamore's conjecture that 0 occurs infinitely often. The proof argues by pigeonhole that the sequence is unbounded, and a new strict record is novel with no larger prior term, so it is followed by 0. Short and elementary, but a correct settlement. Second review: Faithful; proof idea (bounded terms force a value repeated > B+1 times, contradiction; new maxima give zeros) is short but genuine. No prior proof found.

oeis-a343311.note: Israel's conjecture is stated as an iff, faithfully: n is represented iff n is composite and n is not 4, 8, 9 or 25. I brute-forced both sides for n < 400 and they agree. The proof uses the construction p + n/p + (n - p - n/p) from Israel's Maple code, plus case work for squares of primes and small n. Elementary; no earlier proof found. Second review: Faithful and verified to 400; no prior proof found.

oeis-a343913.note: Faithful to Sun's question (MO 391894, no answers). Infinitude is proved by an explicit Pell-type family x = d+y with 7d^2+17 = 12y(d+y), (d,y) -> (17d+12y, 7d+5y). I checked numerically that it gives the solutions m = 71, 34037, 16405581, 7907455823, ... with 2m^2-1 = x^4+y^4 and |x-y| > 1 (71 and 34037 are in the data). I found no prior answer. Second review: Faithful; a neat explicit Pell-orbit family (proof 40 lines) settles Sun's question. The family is visible in the b-file but no one had published it as far as found.

oeis-a344734.note: Faithful (sInf of the positive x with c(n) | 10x+1). The proof computes a(4q+r) explicitly in each residue class (q, 7q+2, 3q+2, 9q+8, with a(1) = 1 the exception), from which the recurrence for n > 9 is immediate (n = 9 fails because of a(1)). Routine. Second review: Faithful; elementary (each residue class mod 4 of the index gives a linear formula). Routine.

oeis-a345003.note: The definitions follow the cited entries (rational-valued where they divide). The proof factors A344998 - A344999 = (D - P)(sigma(n) - 2n), so terms are perfect numbers or numbers with n' = psi(n). Disjointness handles even perfect numbers via Euler's form, and hypothetical odd ones by parity (D odd, P even). Elementary but complete; A345043 only says 'seems to be a multiple of A033879'. Second review: Faithful and true by a two-line factorisation from the definitions in the entries, plus a parity argument for odd perfect numbers. Routine.

oeis-a348598.note: Statement faithfully quantifies over consecutive primes a<b of the form k^2+1 and the overall least qualifying p (p == a mod q, p>a, q>a, both k^2+1 primes). The disproof at a=17 (next term 37) is correct: the least such p is 42437 = 206^2+1 = 17 + 420*101 with q=101, smaller than a(3)=90001 for q=37. I recomputed this independently. A genuine counterexample to Lagneau's conjecture; no earlier refutation found. Second review: Genuine finite counterexample at the third pair: the least qualifying prime uses modulus 101, not 37. The literal reading is the natural one; the disproof does not exploit a typo. Finite check, so routine.

oeis-a350191.note: Statement encodes rooks on triangular/hexagonal boards in barycentric coordinates. Triangle classes are under arbitrary lattice isometries of the placement, which matches A350191's convention as distinguished from A350041 in Kotesovec's n=10 PDF and Brobecker's note. Hexagon classes are under the 12 board symmetries with 2n-1 rooks (A309260). The data agree (1,1,1,5,29,224,3012 at n=1,4,...,19). Brobecker's PDF and the entries give only computations, and no prior proof was found. Second review: Proof: coordinate-sum counting (the IMO 2009 Shortlist C2 / Nivasch-Lev argument) forces every maximum placement on side 3m+1 into the central hexagon, and full occupancy pins any congruence to a hexagon symmetry. The key step is the equality case of a well-known olympiad bound, so this is a short argument from known facts (routine), but I found no prior statement of Kotesovec's conjecture as proved.

oeis-a350557.note: Statement matches Schulte's conjecture: M(n,k)=(-1)^(n-k)T(n,k) with T from the A350557 name formula, L = A350512, and both L*M and M*L are the identity. Exact check for n,k<20. No mention of the inverse in A350512, and no prior proof found. Routine triangular-matrix identity. Second review: Matrix-inverse identity proved from the entry's own recurrence T(n,k)=binom(n-1,k-1)+(2n-1)T(n-1,k) and A350512's binomial structure. Routine triangle identity; no earlier proof found.

oeis-a276752.note: The composition-sum definitions of the log and exp coefficients reproduce the OEIS data (I checked integrality and terms to n=70). oeis-a346126.note: Faithful reading: Pfoertner's 'hexagonal lattice' is the 6-neighbour (triangular) lattice (A346123 covers the honeycomb), disks are taken in the matching metric, closed walks have length >= 3, and the claim is that at every term m >= 2 every optimal walk is closed. oeis-a346659.note: Faithful (r prime with neither r-2 nor r+2 a product of two primes, p = q allowed); the definition reproduces the listed data. Infinitude: every prime r == 173 (mod 225) has 9 | r-2 and 25 | r+2, so neither can be a semiprime other than 9 or 25. Then Dirichlet (Nat.forall_exists_prime_gt_and_modEq) finishes. Short and standard. Second review: Faithful; settled by a three-line covering-class + Dirichlet argument (40-line proof). Easy but no earlier written proof found.

oeis-a347409.note: Faithful. Unaccelerated Collatz traces ending at 1, and the maximal halving run equal to k, for k >= 4 (k <= 3 occurs only finitely often, since every trajectory ends with 16 -> 1 or is a power of 2). The proof builds infinitely many starts by an explicit backward construction. It does not depend on the Collatz conjecture, since only starts with a known trajectory are counted. Elementary. Second review: Faithful; constructive infinite families. No prior proof found.

oeis-a351415.note: Faithful: the intersection of the Beatty sequences for phi and sqrt(5) with positive indices, gaps in {2..6}, and each gap infinitely often. oeis-a351933.note: Mathar's D-finite recurrence for n >= 4 follows from the first-order linear ODE with polynomial coefficients satisfied by exp(x/(1-x^2/2)). oeis-a354672.note: Faithful: squarefree part via the unique D with x^2-1 = D s^2, and cos(m*arccos k) read as T_m(k). The equivalence is the classical fact that Pell solutions are powers of the fundamental one with x-coordinates T_n(x_1), plus a short check that T_m(k) has the same squarefree kernel as k^2-1. The entry even links Wikipedia's Chebyshev/Pell section. Correct and routine. Second review: Faithful; a short consequence of standard Pell theory. No prior written proof found.

oeis-a356334.note: Faithful (pairs x <= y of nonnegative integers, counted with ncard; the solution set is finite). I recomputed a(0..10) = 1, 3, 4, 3, 3, 3, ..., matching the data. The proof classifies the solutions as (0,0), (0,1), (2^(n-1), 2^(n-1)) for n >= 1, n != 2, via a gcd/coprimality argument with odd and even cases. Elementary but not trivial. Searches (MSE, MO, web) found no prior proof. Second review: Faithful; no prior proof found.

oeis-a357127.note: Disproof of the conjunction 'Conjecture 1 and Conjecture 2'. Announce it as 'Conjecture 2 is false'; Conjecture 1 (kept in the conjunction) is actually true by a short argument and is not settled by this proof. Routine finite check.

oeis-a357315.note: Faithful (k ranges over 0 < k < m). Elementary and correct; no prior proof found. Second review: Faithful; short CRT argument, no prior proof found.

oeis-a395839.note: Hanna's parity and mod-3 conjectures are stated faithfully, with a(n)=10*Cat(n+1)-Cat(n). Parity reduces to the classical fact that Cat(n) is odd iff n=2^k-1. The mod-3 clauses follow from C^2-C = X*C^3 = X*C(X^3) mod 3 (Frobenius). No earlier proof of these clauses for this entry found. Routine. Second review: Follows quickly from known Catalan congruences (parity: C(n) odd iff n+1 is a power of 2).

oeis-a396093.note: Both of Hanna's parity conjectures for the third iterate of x/(1-x)^2 are stated faithfully: a(2n) even, and a(2n-1) even iff n=5k-2. Mod 2, B(x)=x/(1+x^2), so the iterate is a rational function over GF(2) with periodic coefficient parity. No earlier proof found in the libraries or the entry. Routine. Second review: Parity of coefficients of a rational g.f.; finite periodicity check.

oeis-a397347.note: Hanna's conjecture a(n) == [1,3,3,3] (mod 4) is stated faithfully. Any integer sequence satisfying the l.g.f. identity, with the x-coefficient fixed at 1, must follow the pattern. Second review: Mod 4 pattern of Hanna's l.g.f.; short induction from the defining recurrence.

oeis-a397588.note: Hanna's parity conjecture (a(n) odd iff n is a power of 2) is stated faithfully for the unique series with A = X + (X A^2)'. Mod 2 the equation becomes B = X + B^2, and Frobenius gives B = X + X^2 + X^4 + ... . No earlier proof found. Routine. Second review: Two-line parity argument from Manyama's recurrence in the entry.

oeis-a397780.note: Disproof of Voievoda's count. The site formalization is faithful: each digit support with an eligible witness contributes exactly one term, its least witness. The proof certifies 671 distinct eligible supports, more than the conjectured 665, including 36 four-digit supports against the conjectured 31. Some witnesses lie beyond the 10^18 search bound stated in the entry. No earlier refutation found. Non-routine: it needs a search for large witnesses. Second review: Disproof by explicit witnesses (finite check). Genuine author miscount, not an index slip: the 4-digit witnesses are all < 10^17, inside the author's claimed exhaustive range.

oeis-a398343.note: Pirc's conjecture that each value m occurs only finitely often is stated faithfully as finiteness of {k>0 : sum_{d|k} rad(d) = m*rad(k)}. Since sum_{d|p^e} rad(d) = 1+e*p, the condition is prod(1+e_p*p) = m*prod p. The proof bounds exponents and prime choices and uses a well-quasi-order argument. No earlier proof found. Second review: Finiteness of fibres of the radical-divisor quotient; no prior proof found.

oeis-a398920.note: Bevan's asymptotic a(n) = n^2 log^2 n/4 + O(n^2 log n) is stated faithfully. The substitution i=b, j=b+d turns the count into #{i<j, a, c >= 1 : ia+jc <= N}, which matches the entry's ab+bc+cd <= n. The proof is elementary harmonic-sum estimation. The leading term also follows from the classical Ingham/Estermann asymptotics for sum d(k)d(n-k). No earlier proof for this entry found. Routine. Second review: True and provable by a short argument from the A002133 g.f. plus the Dirichlet divisor estimate. New as a formal result, but easy.

oeis-a401673.note: Ryłko's conjecture T(n,n^2)=1 and T(n,n^2-1)=n^2(n+1) is formalized faithfully. Tilings are fixed-point-free involutions with displacement at most 1, and crossing diagonals are allowed as in the source. Exactly 4 ordinary cells means two dominoes. Ryłko's own notes say both are observations on rows n<=10, not proofs, and I found no other proof. Second review: Endpoint counts of Ryłko's domicule triangle; the author explicitly calls them unproved observations.

oeis-a401897.note: Sharma's asymptotic a(n) ~ 48n/Pi^2 is stated faithfully: rank is the position in the norm-then-b order of the sector 0<=b<=a, and visibility is coprimality of the coordinate differences over the open disk N(w)<N(z), with w=0 included. The heuristic (density 6/Pi^2 of primitive vectors times area pi*N, with N ~ 8n/pi) matches. The proof does a uniform Möbius lattice-point count. No earlier proof found. Second review: Asymptotic for visible Gaussian integers; plausible (6/pi^2 density, sector 1/8 of disk) and proved.

oeis-a225034.note: Berselli's P-recurrence (n+1)a(n)-(2n+3)a(n-1)-3(n-2)a(n-2)=0 for n>1 is stated faithfully, with a(n) defined combinatorially (101-avoiding words, n ones, at most n zeros). It also follows mechanically from the entry's algebraic g.f., a theorem of Bilotta et al. and Merlini–Nocentini, whose radicand factors as (1-x)^2(1+x)(1-3x). The site proof instead counts words directly. Not in isitsolved or the libraries. Routine. Second review: P-recurrence from the proven algebraic g.f.; routine.

oeis-a346784.note: Disproof of 'covered point count = A346126(n-1)' at n=10. The listed radii (…, 7/3, 13/4, …) skip r^2=3, so the entry's data appears to miss a term. The conjecture matches only that defective list. I reproduced the record sequence numerically; Lean certifies the 13/14 bounds. No earlier report found. Second review: Genuine disproof: 13 is a point-record but not a walk-record, so the correspondence fails. Note it rests on an omission in A346784's own data (missing term 3/1 between 7/3 and 13/4), which the owner may want to report to OEIS.

oeis-a387243.note: The conjecture a(n) = A382131(n) - n is formalized faithfully. A381767(m) is the least N with m^m <= N^(m-1) (= ceil(m^(m/(m-1)))), and A382131 is its complement. The definitions reproduce the data (1,1,2,11,41,130 vs 2,3,5,15,46,136). I found no prior proof in the entries or elsewhere. The argument is short: (k+n)^k < (k+1)^(k+1) iff k+n < c(k+1), c increases by at least 1 each step (an elementary convexity inequality), and complement counting finishes it. Second review: Faithful statement of Boddorf's identity; no prior proof found.

oeis-a389425.note: Sulaiman's conjecture (gaps of A199716 are 1 with natural density 1) is formalized faithfully. 'eligible' requires 6k-5 and 6k-1 to be composite (>1 and not prime), which reproduces 16, 20, 21, ... I found no prior proof. It is a routine consequence of the primes having density zero: the non-eligible k have density 0, so almost every eligible k is followed by an eligible k+1 (130-line proof). Second review: Density-1 claim follows from pi(x)=o(x); faithful, routine.

oeis-a391629.note: Wiseman's conjecture a(n) = A000041(n) - A368684(n) is formalized faithfully: weakly increasing parts must equal the first sums of a weakly decreasing positive sequence, and A368684 is by its name. It reproduces a(6)=9, for instance. I found no prior proof (trureturing has only the sister A391620). Routine: the first sums of a decreasing sequence are decreasing, so the increasing target is constant. That leaves k equal parts with k=1 or n/k even, which is exactly the divisor set A368684 counts. Second review: Wiseman's conjectured formula; faithful, no earlier proof located.

oeis-a393858.note: Both Hanna conjectures (a(n) odd iff n is a power of 2; a(n) == 1 mod 7) are formalized faithfully. Routine: mod 2 the equation becomes A(x - x^2) = x (Catalan numbers, odd iff n is a power of 2), and mod 7 it becomes A(x + xA(-x)) = x with solution x/(1-x). Uniqueness over each residue field finishes it. Second review: Hanna's two congruence conjectures; faithful; no prior proof found.

oeis-a394761.note: Chapman's conjecture (at most eight 1's, four 2's and three 3's in a row) is formalized via 9/5/4 consecutive runs at spacing len+1. I found no prior proof (entry, A392200/A391446, Epoch OEIS Open, Lean libraries, web). The 384-line proof is a genuine residue analysis of A381466. Second review: Disproof by explicit counterexample (nine consecutive 1's at around step 1.95e7), independently reproduced. A finite check, so routine.

mo-461674.note: Faithful in quantile coordinates: laws with the same mean are monotone f, g on (0,1); 'below' is equal mean plus put-price domination, which is the convex order. The conclusion's coupling cost equal to the integral of |f-g|^p gives W_p(lambda,rho) <= W_p(mu,nu), so g(d)=d works for every p>=1, answering the question affirmatively. The construction picks l pointwise from {f,g} with prefix integrals equal to the max, and r = f+g-l. No MO answer exists (only comments). No earlier solution found. Second review: Positive answer with g = identity; short but genuine argument; no earlier answer found.

The site disproves it at n = 2^(2^22+2) via a Halasz-type L1 discrepancy (Riesz product) bound against the balanced-side pigeonhole. arXiv v3 (2026-07-22) still lists it as open. The Halasz idea is the statement contributor's remark, not prior literature. Substantive negative answer; no earlier solution found. Second review: Genuine disproof of Open Question 1 (no 2-balanced sequence for a specific huge n). No prior settlement found.

Because the evaluation identity holds for all t and y, F is uniquely determined, so natDegree is the true degree. The question has no answers and its comments give no proof (StackExchange API). The 315-line proof is a genuine argument (norm pairing, binomial series, Laurent coefficients). Second review: Faithful; no prior answer.

oeis-a228916.note: Kotesovec's conjecture (indices n>1 of primes in A108300 are multiples of 3) is stated faithfully, with u(0)=1, u(1)=5, u(n)=3u(n-1)+u(n-2). The proof is an elementary covering: u(m) mod 10 has period 12, u(m) is even for m=2 mod 3, and 5 divides u(m) for m=1 mod 3, with m=1 (u=5) the lone exception. No prior proof was found, but the argument is routine. Second review: Conjecture follows from u mod 10 periodicity; routine.

oeis-a332553.note: Sloane's Conjectures 1 and 2 (records of n/a(n) occur exactly at T_j-1 with value j/2+1, and a(n) > 2n/(j+2) below T_j-1) are formalized faithfully, with A082183/A082184 by sInf; this reproduces the data. Numerically the records for n<3000 are exactly n=2,5,9,14,20,... with values j/2+1. oeis-a182129.note: Lagneau's generalization (every orbit of k -> (digit sum of k)^n eventually repeats) is stated faithfully. Second review: Lagneau's 'conjecture' is trivial (orbit bounded). Note: oeis-a178481 on this site states the same conjecture (conjugate map), proved 13 s later.

mo-459462.note: Englander asks whether q(n,k)=S_2(n,k)/S(n,k) is strictly decreasing in k. Second review: Row 6 of Hardin's A201042; the claim is a degree-6 polynomial count, which Ehrhart theory makes expected but nobody had written down for this row. Routine polynomial/g.f. identity.

oeis-a079953.note: Mathar's conjecture A079953(n)=A039734(n) (n>=2) is stated faithfully: the least prime q with p mod 2q = p is the unique prime below p maximizing p mod q. The proof needs a prime in (3v/4, v] for v>=11, proved from Chebyshev-type lcm bounds plus a finite chain. Numerically it holds for all primes below 2*10^5. No prior proof was found in the entries or the libraries. Second review: Proof: a prime in (3v/4, v] (Chebyshev/Nagura style) gives q0 <= 2p/3 so p mod q0 >= p/3, while primes below p/2 leave remainders < p/3. Short argument from a known prime-gap theorem; genuinely settles Mathar's conjecture.

oeis-a317850.note: Thomas's 'iff n = 3, 7, 15 (mod 20)' is refuted at n=4. g(a)=(a^4+1)^4+1-a has the root a=2 mod 10 with derivative a unit mod 10, so Hensel gives a 10-adic pair x = ...2, y = x^4+1. I lifted it to 20 digits (x = ...696407492162, y = ...828975851537, and y^4+1 = x). The 10-adic encoding is faithful (compatible families in ZMod 10^k, n>=1). This is a genuine but routine Hensel counterexample to the printed claim. Second review: Disproof: at n=4 there is a 10-adic 2-cycle x = ...2, y = x^4+1 (Hensel, derivative a unit mod 10). Many other n outside {3,7,15 mod 20} also work, so Thomas's conjecture is simply false. Finite Hensel check, hence routine.

oeis-a363473.note: Both the permutation conjecture and the generalized b-version are formalized faithfully (BijOn from {1<=k<=n} onto the positive integers). It is routine by unique factorization: for k>=2, T(n,k)=k*p with p a prime >= gpf(k), so every composite m arises exactly once (k = m/gpf(m), with n fixed by the index of gpf(m)), and column 1 gives 1 and the primes. The same argument works with b(k) in place of k. No prior proof was found. Second review: Both conjectures follow from the unique factorisation m = (m/gpf(m))*gpf(m); a short elementary argument. Faithful and true, low novelty.

oeis-a390217.note: Hutton's conjectured g.f. (1/4)(P(x)^4 + P(x^2)^2 + 2P(x^4)) for 4-colored partitions with color sum = 0 mod 4 is stated faithfully. Multiplicity vectors are bounded by n, products are truncated at range n (enough for coefficient n), and a(0)=1. It is a routine roots-of-unity filter: at omega=i the four color factors give 1/(1-x^(4j)), and at omega=-1 they give 1/(1-x^(2j))^2. No prior proof was found. Second review: Standard roots-of-unity filter (Burnside) proof of the conjectured g.f.; true and faithful, routine g.f. identity.

oeis-a227720.note: Kimberling's recurrence and g.f. The printed recurrence's -2a(n-1) is a sign typo: it fails on the data (gives -321 at n=7), while the printed g.f. denominator implies +2a(n-1). The statement uses the g.f.-consistent sign and the printed g.f. unchanged, a faithful repair that the proof does not exploit. The proof bounds log to show 1/s(n) lies in [3n^2+(9n+1)/4, +1/4), giving a(n)=3n^2+floor((9n+1)/4); I confirmed this for n<3000 at 50 digits. Routine. Second review: Kimberling's g.f. holds: rounding of a quasi-polynomial with period 4 whose fractional offsets stay away from 1/2. Routine after log bounds; the typo correction is correctly documented.

oeis-a007528.note: Valianatos' conjecture, with the n-th primes = 5 mod 6 paired against the n-th primes = 1 mod 6 and partial products tending to 3/4, is stated faithfully. Numerically the product is 0.750034 after 928739 pairs. The value is L(1,chi_-3)^2/L(2,chi_0) with the p=2 factor removed, and the pairing is handled by a(n)/b(n) -> 1. The 922-line proof establishes this convergence; no prior written proof was found in the entry or the libraries. Second review: True and faithful. It is a short consequence of classical facts (Euler product at s=1, value of L(1,chi) mod 6, index pairing harmless by density), so low novelty; the Lean proof does the analytic work from scratch.

oeis-a270923.note: Kotesovec's conjectured limit a(n)^(1/n^2) -> exp(exp(-1)) is refuted. Using r^3 <= 3^r (r^(1/r) is maximal at r=3 over the integers), every term is at most poly(n)^n * 3^(n^2/3), so limsup <= 3^(1/3) = 1.44225 < exp(1/e) = 1.44467. The conjecture used the real maximizer e instead of the integer 3. The finite multiplicity-sum definition reproduces the data 1,2,10,88,1414,46648,3026028,373615284 (my check). Genuine, short refutation. Second review: Kotesovec's conjectured constant e^(1/e) is the real maximum of k^(1/k); with integer part sizes the maximum is 3^(1/3), so the conjecture is false. Elementary bound, routine. The same error sits in A252782 and A270917 (A270917 is also disproved on the site).

oeis-a002105.note: Bala's conjecture (reduced tangent numbers mod k are eventually periodic with period dividing phi(k)) is stated faithfully as a(n+phi(k)) = a(n) mod k for n >= N. The proof uses von Staudt-Clausen for powers of 2 and an exponential-sum model for odd moduli, and its header says the method adapts the site's earlier proof for A002439 (Glaisher's T numbers, a different sequence and claim). So this is not a duplicate. No prior proof of this specific claim was found, though it is in the spirit of classical Kummer-type congruences. Second review: Settles Bala's conjecture for this entry, with the 2-part from von Staudt-Clausen and odd moduli by the same exponential-sum method as Kallat (2026) and the site's A002439 proof. Not literally covered by prior work, but close to a routine adaptation.

oeis-a112971.note: Barry's four conjectures a(2^n)=a(2^(n+1)+1)=A005578(n), a(2^n-1)=a(3*2^n-1)=1 are stated faithfully for all n>=0, with the Riordan array (1,xc(x)) squared and reduced mod 2 entrywise. oeis-a227071.note: Schmidt's conjecture a(n+1)=A132741(n)+1 (n>=1) is stated faithfully: 'k^m ends with k' is read as k^m mod 10^len(k) = k, and a(n) is the least m>=1 with s(m)=s(n). Proof: s(n+1) depends only on 2^v2(n)*5^v5(n), shown with CRT and orders mod 2^D, 5^D, plus explicit separating witnesses k. That is real number theory, not a definitional unfolding. The companion A227070 conjecture (a(n+1)=A003592(n)+1) is closely related but separate; it is not a duplicate on this site.

mse-5025318.note: Faithful: polynomials with rational coefficients (no loss for integer-valued ones) mapping N^2 into Z^2, with surjectivity asked; the disproof shows no such surjection exists. Argument: clear denominators by d, take q=d(x+d+1)+1 coprime to d, so the map is surjective and hence bijective on (Z/q)^2. Then the preimage (x,y) of d*F(-d,0) must be congruent to (-d,0), contradicting 0<x+d<q. The question has no answers (only comments calling it hard), linked siblings are unanswered, and no prior solution was found. Short but genuinely new. Second review: A correct, fairly short disproof, and the question has no answer on MSE. No prior source found.

oeis-a337742.note: Yashin's a(2n)=2a(n) is stated faithfully as the minimal period of the pair (previous, current) under current' = rot(previous XOR current) from the single-bit seed. No earlier proof found in the entry, the Lean libraries, Blanco Gomez or the isitsolved map. The characteristic-2 doubling argument is standard in spirit but the conjecture had been open since 2020. oeis-a193662.note: Mathar's recurrence a(n)=2a(n-1)+3a(n-2)-4a(n-3) (n>3) is stated faithfully. The Q-residue (all t(i,j)=1) of the Lucas polynomials reduces to a(n)=sum [x^k]L(n,x) r(n-k) with r(k)=2^(k-1); my computation reproduces the data and the recurrence through n=19. Proof via 2^n L(n,1/2) and the constant leading coefficient. The sister A193649 (solved on the site separately) does not imply it. Routine. Second review: Faithful. Routine rational g.f. identity.

oeis-a112290.note: Kotesovec's limit (the reduced fraction sum_{k=1..n} 1/S(n,k) tends to 2) is stated faithfully; numerator/denominator in lowest terms equals the sum. It is elementary: the k=1 and k=n terms are 1, and each of the n-2 interior terms is at most 1/C(n,2), so they contribute at most 2/(n-1). No earlier proof found. Correct but routine, close to trivial. Second review: Faithful, true by a short argument. Routine.

oeis-a111869.note: Corneth's Conjecture 1 (for odd primes p, the least k with p^2 | C(2k,k) is (p^2-1)/2+1) is stated faithfully. By Kummer, p^2 | C(2k,k) iff adding k+k in base p carries at least twice. The least such k has digits ((p-1)/2, (p+1)/2), i.e. k=(p^2+1)/2, and the central coefficient there is twice an odd multiple of p^2. Only Conjecture 1 is formalized (Conjectures 2 and 3 are not claimed). Elementary; no earlier proof found. Second review: Faithful. Follows directly from Kummer's theorem. Routine.

oeis-a103528.note: Kurkov's 2022 formula 2a(n) = b(n)-b(n-1)-1 (n>1), with b(n)=sum_{k<=floor(log2 n)} c(n-k,k) and c(t,k)=t-(t mod 2^k), is stated faithfully (index shift j=k-1, a(1)=0). I checked it numerically for n<3000. Proof: each rounding c(n-k,k) jumps by 2^k exactly when n == k (mod 2^k). No earlier proof found; routine. Second review: Faithful. Routine identity.

oeis-a130896.note: Barker's g.f. (denominator (1-x)^3(1+x)^3(1+x^2)^3 = (1-x^4)^3) and the recurrence a(n)=3a(n-4)-3a(n-8)+a(n-12) for n>12 are stated faithfully for the explicitly defined quadruples {2m+1,2m+1,4m,(2m+1)m}. mo-313670.note: Abdollahi's conjecture (support size of a right annihilator of 1+x+y or 1+x-y in C[G], G finite, bounds exp<x,y>) is stated faithfully. The question has no answers. Second review: A correct disproof via finite quotients of the (2,3,6) triangle group. The 3-term question is unanswered on MO, and I found no prior refutation.

mo-248883.note: The question asks: in S_n (7<=n<=10), if H1 = S_k and H2 = S_{n-k} commute elementwise, must they be point stabilizers? The disproof gives n=7, k=2: H1 = <(0 1)> and H2 = {sigma * (0 1)^{sign sigma} : sigma in S_5 on letters 2..6}, a twisted copy of S_5 that commutes with H1 but is not a pointwise stabilizer. Schlage-Puchta's answer only shows H1 is a stabilizer when a prime lies in (n/2, n-k], and the comments' counterexamples are for n=6 (outside the range). The negative answer is new to the thread but the construction is a routine sign twist. Second review: Disproof by the sign-twisted embedding of S_5 into S_2 x S_5 inside S_7. It answers the question as asked (no), using a standard trick that the thread missed; elementary, finite.

mo-257393.note: Irreducibility of p and q_0 over the fraction field K of C[x_1..x_l]/(q_1..q_{l-1}); the indexing (l=m+1, z_0..z_l, x_1..x_k in p) matches the question, and the primality of I is assumed exactly as the asker allows. Unanswered on MO (no answers or comments); no prior proof found. mo-397080.note: No dimension-free constant C exists, even in the asker's limsup form; the counterexample uses diagonal positive contractions and a unitary reflection. Ramps, normalized trace norm and quantifiers match the question. The comments cite Connes (Annals 1976, Remark 1.2.7) only for the variant with an arbitrary positive B instead of U*AU, so the unitary-conjugate case settled here was not covered. Second review: Negative answer: no k-independent constant exists, even for the limsup. A multiscale Householder construction, numerically confirmed; new as far as I can tell.

mo-420936.note: Answers the soft question: no uniform c gives B >= c*t_2^{q1}*t_1^{q2} (counterexample with diagonal invertible matrices), together with a sharp power-mean lower bound in t_2 alone, using sigma_1 >= sqrt(sigma_1 sigma_2). The statement handles the question's 3-versus-4 index slip by covering every family size >= 2. Elementary; unanswered on MO. Second review: Answers a loosely posed question: no constant multiple of t2*t1 bounds B from below, with an alternative power-mean bound. Elementary; low novelty.

mo-472881.note: Parts (a),(b) are Lagrange interpolation (as Vit Tucek's comment notes); for (c) the statement adopts a strong reading (every coefficient polynomial in v on the admissible locus, no uniform degree bound) and proves it impossible. In essence, letting v->0, a point fixed by all of Gamma, forces p(0)=1 and p(0)=0. A commenter says (c) is under-specified, so this settles one reasonable reading. Elementary. Second review: Answers yes to (a),(b) and no to (c) by a scaling argument. Faithful to the clarified question, short proof.

mo-332685.note: Shows Spielman's bound is sharp at alpha+beta+delta+epsilon=1 with E=Y+X-1, P=XY on the grids {0,1}x{0,1}: all eight local divisibilities hold (P vanishes on two of the lines) but E does not divide P.
